article_title: How to put together a work outfit that you actually like
sub_title: Sommyyah Awan, Katrina O'Shea and Daribha Lyndem break down their approach to putting together a chic work outfit
article_content: If you’ve ever found yourself at the receiving end of a “This is a school, not a fashion show” reprimand because your skirt was hitched an inch too high, entering the corporate world as an adult can dredge up some embarrassing memories. Unless, of course, you were to make the office your runway. The average officegoer spends a significant amount of their life under fluorescent lights, shuffling between meetings and coffee runs, before slowly dissolving into monotony. So if the corporate world insists on consuming most of your waking hours, the least it can do is bear witness to a fabulous fit. It’s time to shake up those tired corporate dress codes and take a leaf out of the books of these three professionals. “I’m in the office four to five times a week from 9 to 5, that’s a considerable amount of my life,” shares Awan. “If I look my best, I feel good. I work in an environment where I never know who I’m going to meet. And every encounter is an opportunity for a great first impression.” Awan gravitates towards tailoring—suits, Accessories are where Awan has fun, “I love Awan's work outfit staples include: Finance isn’t known for encouraging fashion risks, but O’Shea has carved out a style that feels both personal and unfussy. Her philosophy is simple: start where you are. “It doesn’t have to be zero to a hundred,” she says. “You can introduce pieces gradually and see how they make you feel and how they’re received.” Those small choices build confidence. “If it feels right, keep going,” she says. “Even something small like a sculptural For O’Shea, practicality is important: “If you’re already running late and you’ve got to pull an ironing board out, it’s game over,” she says. Comfort, however, can be negotiated. “I often sacrifice comfort if it means the outfit comes together beautifully. I commute in heels more often than I should, but at the same time, comfort and style don’t have to be mutually exclusive.” Her wardrobe reflects that reality: wide-leg trousers, crisp shirts and O’Shea is also firmly anti-trend. “One of my greatest fears is walking into a room wearing the same thing as someone else,” she says. “I’d have no choice but to go home.” That approach has helped her build a wardrobe she actually enjoys. “It makes getting dressed exciting,” she says. “It feels like I’m constantly inventing and reinventing.” Crucially, her clothes haven’t undermined her credibility. “Once people see that your professionalism and output are unaffected by how you dress, those preconceptions fade away.” O'Shea's work outfit staples include: Lyndem’s approach to office dressing is uncomplicated. “The day I want to wear neutrals, I’ll wear neutrals,” she says. “The day I want to be colourful, I’ll wear colourful clothes.” Her style is eclectic, intuitive and driven by mood rather than rules. “Sometimes the colour combinations I choose are something I’ve just seen on the street, like the wall outside a shop and its shutters. Colour is everywhere in India, so it’s quite easy.” Experimentation is key. “You’re just going to have to mix and match and try everything,” she says. “You try everything and make do with whatever you have. If I see something trendy or something I like, I’ll get it stitched,” she explains, which allows her to personalise trends rather than replicate them. That same mindset carries into traditional wear. article_content: For a recent press tour, Keerthy Suresh stepped out in a styling choice that reflects a larger shift in Indian occasion wear. She opted for a velvet kurta by RajiRamniq with blue At the centre of her look is a lime-green kurta from RajiRamniq’s ‘Nisbat’ collection, which draws from the idea of connection between craft and contemporary life. According to designers Raji Sharma and Ramniq Tangri Khatri, “crafted in a luminous velvet fabric, the kurta features a fluid straight silhouette with side slits for movement and modernity. The rich lime-green hue brings depth and royalty, while the relaxed structure keeps it breathable, wearable and celebration-ready.” A closer look at the kurta reveals its dense and layered craftsmanship. “The piece comes alive through an amalgamation of traditional embellishment like pearls, zardozi, Resham and metal coins in a modern, contemporary design,” the designers explain. “In the Nisbat collection, each element is applied through a carefully staged, hand-led process. Resham embroidery frames the borders and establishes definition. Zardozi adds architectural depth. Pearl work introduces softness and a subtle sheen, while mirror work is intentionally restrained to enhance light and movement. Metal coins at the neckline function as a tactile, heritage-inspired detail,” the duo elaborates about the surface ornamentation that took approximately 48 to 60 artisanal hours. “One of the understated strengths of the kurta lies in its versatility. While the craftsmanship gives it a ceremonial presence, the silhouette is intentionally balanced to move easily across contexts. It can be paired with a velvet sharara for formal settings or worn effortlessly with denims for a relaxed, contemporary look, much like Keerthy Suresh did,” they add. Leaning fully into the bohemian mood, the actor extended the aesthetic through her accessories, opting for a choker and earrings from Binni, a floral silver ring from Abhilasha Jewelry Collection, and another from Keiyura Jewelry. Her hippy fishtail braid was finished with oxidised accents from Rubans Jewellery, while smoky kohled eyes and nude lips completed the look. For footwear, she picked a pair of heels from Fizzy Goblet, adorned with embroidery that mirrored the crafts on her kurta.

article_title: Samantha Ruth Prabhu’s pistachio Banarasi silk sari is hand-beaten patua zari
sub_title: The actor paired her Label Sourav Das drape with emerald jewellery
article_content: On Republic Day, Samantha Ruth Prabhu made her way to the Rashtrapati Bhavan for the At Home reception after receiving an invite from President Droupadi Murmu. For the occasion, the south star wore heritage on her sleeves, turning to a revival Banarasi Iktara weave from the Label Sourav Das. Rendered in a pistachio green that looks time-honoured yet freshly calibrated for now, the sari breaks from the primary jewel tones typically associated with Banarasi drapes. The silk canvas is scattered with gold woven buttis, while a rich border and pallu elevates it. “Samantha’s is wearing a quintessential Hazar Buiti Asharfi Sikka revival Banarasi sari with a bygone angri border woven in finer counts of mulberry silk. It also has konias on either side of the pallu. The sari is woven with Kaduwa method in Iktara style with hand-beaten patua zari,” shares Sourav Das. The Iktara, also known as single thread, technique offers not just strength and smoothness but also a fluid fall and a resilient life that’s prized by connoisseurs. Banarasi saris have long occupied a rarefied place in Indian wardrobes. Their lineage traces back centuries of royal patronage and painstaking craftsmanship. One weave can take weeks, sometimes months, to complete, with master weavers translating complex designs onto looms that demand memory and muscle. What makes them singular is not just the silk or the zari, but the varied motifs, from florals nodding to abundance, to paisley border, signifying fertility and eternity. In the actor’s sari, the geometric buttis, which speaks of cosmic order, feels particularly resonant. It serves an emblem of continuity for a woman who has repeatedly chosen longevity over trend. She completed the look with an open-setting diamond and emerald choker, complemented by matching stud earrings and a statement ring from Golecha’s Jewels. Her hair was worn in a sleek, middle-parted half-up, half-down style, while her makeup stayed understated and refined with a matte, skin-like base, softly smoked eyes and a nude lip that let the jewellery and weave take the spotlight. A pistachio sari and jewels, like hers, is a smart trousseau investment. While it is timeless in spirit, it is refreshingly modern and versatile enough to move seamlessly from intimate family ceremonies to landmark events for years to come.

article_title: A life beautifully lived—Hamish Bowles remembers Valentino
sub_title: Valentino Garavani conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a certain idea of beauty to all he touched
article_content: Valentino Clemente Ludovico Garavani—known, simply and powerfully, as Valentino—was born on May 11th, 1932, in Voghera, a rather quiet place lost somewhere between Milan and Genoa. But by the time he died, aged 93, on January 19, he had conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a “I love beauty—it’s not my fault,” Valentino famously said with a shrug, and in fashion, he saw a way to captivate and ensnare women (his only clients when starting out, before he widened the purview of his well-dressed net). He trained at the Accademia dell’Arte in Milan, studying both French and fashion, and then, aged 17, moved to Paris, to the École des Beaux-Arts and the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture, before securing an apprenticeship in 1951 with the Athenian couturier Jean Dessès, who dressed royalty and high society ladies in his immaculately draped and vividly colored evening gowns. Jacqueline, the Comtesse de Ribes, dressed with Dessès, and when she was asked by Oleg Cassini to design some dresses for him in Paris, she mentioned it to Dessès, telling the designer that “I don’t know how to draw in a chic way.” Dessès was amused. “I have an Italian illustrator,” he told her, “who would be very happy to earn a little more money after working-hours doing the drawings for you”, and a friendship between Valentino and Jacqueline was born. When he was When Guy Laroche, Dessès’s assistant, departed to start his own couture house, Valentino joined him for a few years before leaving to work briefly with the Russian-Georgian Princess Irene Galitzine (Galitzine had made palazzo pyjamas a thing, amidst opulent evening clothes). Then, in 1959, Valentino started his own house with backing from his father and a family friend. In the meantime, someone had come into his life. Giancarlo Giammetti recently recalled their first meeting, with Giammetti seated alone in a Roman cafe. “A kind person came and said, ‘Are you alone?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ ‘Do you mind if me and my friend can sit here?’ Of course,” Giammetti remembered. “And Valentino sat next to me—I remember very deeply.” A whoosh of dark hair framed Valentino’s tanned face, with its sultry features and his arresting blue eyes. “Then Valentino started to speak to me in French. I said, ‘Sorry?’ ‘Oh, sorry—I just arrived from Paris after seven years, my mind goes French, and I was hoping that you speak French…’” Giammetti, it turns out, had studied French for most of his life. “He said, ‘From now on, if I see you again, we speak French.’ And we still do. Incredibly.” The two would speak French to each other—as lovers, and then as intimate friends and business partners—for the rest of Valentino’s life. Valentino soon found a lavish, frescoed apartment in the fashionable Via Condotti, but less than a year later, he was facing bankruptcy. (Though Valentino threw the blame at his “champagne tastes,” someone had not been paying the rent.) He and Giammetti simply moved the salon to a 16th-century palazzo on the Via Gregoriana. (Incidentally, Giammetti acquired the Via Condotti apartment recently and has had it transformed into his offices by Studio Peregalli’s Laura Sartori Rimini. It’s a sumptuous series of rooms, the walls now hung with silver tissue or silk velvet—though some still have their original frescoes—and filled with Hervé van der Straten furniture and antiques. What may have been “Champagne tastes” in 1959 are now sublime and defining.) Valentino gradually began to make his mark on fashion. His flashing good looks easily summoned the press, to be sure, but it was his clothes that had an allure for the stars who would pass through Rome. And when Elizabeth Taylor, there to shoot Suddenly, his work was appearing in As Valentino became a name to watch, with ladies—Audrey Hepburn, Sophia Loren, any number of princesses, Jaqueline Kennedy Onassis, Nan Kempner, Lynn Wyatt, and Susan Gutfreund, among so many more, flocking to dress with him—so his residences became exponentially more impressive. His Roman base—a penthouse apartment with Persian miniatures on the fabric-covered walls and banquettes fit for a Turkish salon, had been transformed into a house on the Appian Way, decorated by Renzo Mongiardino, the When I first went to Rome for the couture in the mid-’80s, long before my Appian Way adventure, I plucked up all my courage and walked into Valentino’s intimidating couture salon just off the top of the Spanish steps—two small-ish rooms that positively oozed with Of course, this pair of elegantly finished rooms opened onto a positive hive of industry occupying five floors of a vast palazzo. Here were the couture ateliers: room after room of industrious ladies and a smattering of men—hundreds of them—applied to the task at hand in light-flooded rooms. (Some years after my first adventure with the couture salon, the place was subtly transformed by the English architects and designers Peter Moore and Peter Kent—there were silvered bannisters, acres of pale grey marble in the hallways, and paintings by Julian Schnabel, Keith Haring, and Francesco Clemente, and it was all very, very chic.) Valentino’s show then always finished with music just before the In 1991, I had an appointment with Valentino to discuss his entire career, and met with him in an elegant room looking over the Piazza Mignanelli, filled with antiques and lush draperies that lent it a Cécile Sorel sort of look. It was not easy getting him to speak. Next door in a vast room—and I mean Of course, Valentino had a number of other properties: in Capri, in New York, in London. But in 1995, I was invited to the 17th century chateau of brick and stone he had acquired—a house that was revealed to me only after I had followed a drive and dramatically turned a corner: There, plunging downhill, and glimmering below, was the Chateau de Wideville, once home to Madame de la Valliere, mistress of Louis XIV (Versailles is conveniently near). In the evening’s light, I explored the breathtaking Jacques Wirtz gardens, where brilliant violet rosemary stretched across the field and cut through the forests, while roses and scented high-summer flowers filled the walled garden. And then: the breathtaking house itself. Valentino worked with Henri Samuel on the interiors, which—with their emerald silk-velvet armchairs and a sort of Chinoiserie motif, which gave the house a sort of fanciful Palm Beach air—brought a level of comfort to the splendidly austere exterior. I was amused to see that the enormous Francis Bacon in Valentino’s sitting room depicted an abstracted man sitting on a carpet of bunches of roses, quite unlike anything I had seen before in his work—as Valentino-ish as it was possible for a Bacon to be. As I headed in for dinner, rather moved by the exquisite gardens and the ravishing interiors—by everything that Giancarlo and Valentino had done in life—I said to Valentino, “What you’ve done is to create beauty.” He clasped my hand and, weeping, said, “It

article_title: Are you brave enough to wear these ‘ugly jeans’?

article_content: Fashion is an era where one person's ‘absolutely not’ is simply someone else's intrusive thoughts let loose. Whether it's jeans with a triple waistband—straight out of an Austin Powers wardrobe malfunction, or patchwork This isn’t about looking pretty anymore. It’s about audacity and daring to walk out the door like a Bratz doll in obnoxiously knee-high Fashion is temporary. Opinions are fleeting. And the only style that matters is the one that makes you feel alive. Look at it long enough, and it often grows on you—because beauty, after all, lies in the eye of the beholder. Millennials drowned in baggy jeans, so Gen Z could run in wide-leg ones. For people who don't trust handbags. There's nothing like intentionally torn clothes to disappoint your elders. Sometimes, even jeans need a little breathing Sustainability, but slightly confused, for when your past refuses to stay archived. For when you run out of clothes, but have a pair of scissors and some glue. The optical illusion that no one asked for, and yet, here we are. article_title: Shanaya Kapoor’s Anita Dongre lehenga is brought to life with hand-painted Pichhwai
sub_title: Hand-painted flora and fauna move across the surface, layered with antique work that gives the piece a tactile richness
article_content: When it comes to occasionwear, Shanaya Kapoor consistently returns to pieces designed to last. Her latest pick, an Featuring a strappy blouse and a billowing skirt, the ensemble’s silk base lends a diaphanousness that mirrors Kapoor’s pared-back approach to ceremonial dressing. Set against a distinctive meadow greenish-yellow, the lehenga immediately stands apart for its nature-inspired hue. Motifs take centre stage in the look, in sync with Dongre's signature design language. The hand-painted Pichhwai artwork unfolds across the lehenga like a living landscape, populated with blooming florals, foliage, wildlife and fluttering birds. The blouse reflects the same story and is further elevated with intricate surface techniques. A delicate organza dupatta brings the ensemble together, offering a gentler counterpoint to the richly detailed lehenga. The ensemble draws its soul from the art of Pichhwai painting, a 400-year-old craft that originated in Rajasthan in the 16th century. Traditionally created as devotional backdrops depicting tales of Shrinathji, Pichhwai paintings were also deeply inspired by the rhythms of nature, from seasons to flora and fauna. In the lehenga, this heritage is reinterpreted with each motif meticulously hand-painted by skilled artisans and delicately enhanced with sequins. The lehenga took close to 90 days to create, a timeline that honours the patience and attention this craft demands. The piece is animated by an in-house master painter, whose deep-rooted Pichhwai lineage informs every brushstroke. As the designer shared, this lehenga is part of the House of Anita Dongre’s larger effort to ensure that art forms like Pichhwai continue to thrive within a contemporary language. She accessorised with intricate temple jewellery from Indinoor. A gold necklace adorned with bird motifs carried on the lehenga’s avian motifs, paired with statement jhumkas and kaan chains that were attached to her loose braid. For her beauty look, she stuck with dewy makeup in warm copper tones for a soft, sun-kissed finish.

article_title: The digital Vintage Casio watch is bending time in 2025
sub_title: From a certain NYC mayor to your style influencer cousin, simple 20th-century timepieces like Casio’s A1000MA series have become everyone’s go-to accessories.
article_content: As I stand on an uneven platform for the next train, I am presented with my current favourite fashion show—the New York subway. You can spot a fall/winter ’25 And this isn’t just a New York thing. Over the last two months, I’ve started noticing the same glint everywhere I go. In Tokyo, it’s the clear-resin variants; in Seoul, the retro golds; in Mumbai cafés, the classic F91W that refuses to retire. One September afternoon in Bandra, outside a tiny post-production studio, a filmmaking student waited for his auto wearing a block-printed kurta and a gold-toned Casio LA670. A week later in Delhi, during a quick coffee run in Meherchand Market, a If you glance around, you’ll also spot the odd Seiko Rotocall and Q Timex, but somehow, it is vintage Casio watches that are dominating the conversation. Especially, the A1000MA-7—and somehow the entire Casio Vintage family has found itself back in the cultural spotlight. History was first made with the release of the Casiotron (QW02-10) in 1974—the world’s first fully digital wristwatch with an automatic calendar—but it was never just a timekeeper. Over the years, Casio digital watches have become pop-culture fixtures, appearing everywhere from on-screen sci-fi fantasies including They remain a staple of This lineage, from the pioneering Casiotron to the cult-classic F-91W of the 1990s, leads directly to today’s A1000 models. They carry the same retro credibility and matte-metal minimalism, now elevated with polished stainless steel and a Milanese strap. It’s this blend of historic tech cool and modern refinement that makes wearing the watch both disarmingly ordinary and unexpectedly iconic. “It’s one of the few timepieces that slips into anyone’s life without demanding a costume change,” says stylist Ayesha Amin Nigam, who has been spotting them on shoots across Delhi and Mumbai. She tells me that, in the last year alone, she’s seen them on interns, models, production assistants, even accountants who wander on set in between takes. “It shapeshifts into whatever the outfit needs—grounding streetwear, sharpening suiting or sitting quietly against a The variants alone could fill a moodboard: the brushed-steel A1000MA, its gold-toned MG counterpart, the pastel-tinted MPR editions, the ultra-slim LA670s, and even the resin-cased F-series that collectors love for its purist ’80s silhouette. And unlike many vintage icons, most of these models are still in production and available directly at brand stores, while a handful of discontinued colourways and older A1000 batches quietly trade hands on resale platforms like My Almari and Luxepolis for those seeking a deeper There is another reality that also exists: Christie’s Geneva Luxury Week reported sales of 21,641,435 Swiss francs (approximately ₹242 crores) in rare watches, with a significant 34% of the bidders being millennials and Gen Z’ers. If younger consumers are willing to spend big at auction, why are modest, sub-₹20,000 digital Casios suddenly the cultural touchstone? Part of the answer lies in accessibility, nostalgia and the social currency of effortless style. “Casio democratised digital timekeeping long before it was fashionable,” explains Sarosh Mody, founder of Luxury Watch Works, an after-sales boutique based in Mumbai. “The G-Shock, for example, became—and remains—a cultural icon. Its popularity reflects the people’s choice, not marketing, not snob value. Casio understood utility decades before smartwatches were conceived. The calculator, TV, radio and camera watches were made by them way before the Swiss even thought about them. The brand has blurred the line between Today, reissues and collaborations like the Timex T80 x Maison Margiela and Omega x Swatch drops show that design credibility doesn’t need a luxury price tag. Together, these watches have become a global shorthand for personality, nostalgia and style that crosses generations and geographies. And style icons and collectors continue the trend: Casio watches were a mainstay of But why this watch and why now? I suspect that it’s because it is fundamentally reminiscent of a simpler time. The only complication in the watch is an alarm, just like the one you would wear in school, beeping at the end of an exam. It’s something you perhaps spotted on your father back in the day, and till today, it rings a bell. A personal connection in your wardrobe that tells a story: perhaps that’s the ultimate style flex.

article_title: 2025 is the year we pledged allegiance to the tabi shoe
sub_title: The horse hoof-lookalikes are no longer just on the runway—they are also next to you on the Mumbai local.
article_content: In an era of touch-and-go trends, no one would have imagined that shoes that look like horse hooves would have staying power. Back in 2023, when The controversial shoe has always been highly endorsed. In 1988, Let’s just say if you made a drinking game out of every time you saw a certified cool person in tabis, it would not end well for your nervous system. And the bug spreads well beyond celebrities. From the streets of Central Saint Martins in London to the Mumbai local, from Dua Lipa to Naina Bhan to “We’re the first generation with instant access to global fashion. Our appetite to experiment has never been stronger,” says Akanksha Rathore, the founder of lifestyle brand Kilchu. “We saw this as an interesting opportunity to define tabis in the context of Indian juttis.” At Kilchu, you can pick between hand-painted leather styles in aquamarine, salmon or a dark brown that quite literally passes as a horse hoof. That’s not all: even athleisure brands like Nike and Reebok have explored sneakerina split toes. And you know the hype is real when a trend transcends the chronically online and makes it to the glitzy shaadi circuit, as is the case with the golden tabi heels from Chal Jooti. Before you roll your eyes at the dupe-fication of Margiela, it’s essential to note that the tabis were not invented by the French. Their provenance can be traced back to 15th-century Japan, where these were worn as socks, separating the big toe from the rest to maintain grip, balance and comfort. By the early 20th century, rubber soles strengthened the slip ons, creating the style we now call tabis. In fact, the so-called luxury design is still commonly worn by labourers in Japan. Could it be that the internet’s obsession with Hobonichi planners, Studio Ghibli, matcha and all things East Asia summoned the return of the tabis? Well perhaps. But if you ask stylist and designer Jayati Monga, an ardent wearer of the In truth, the central conflict of the tabi—the ‘will they, won’t they’—is a major draw for many wearers. At a time when everything from your inside-joke laptop sticker to the DIY crochet keychain on your bag is a way to script your personality, wearing tabis signals which niche you bend the knee for. It is a strange IYKYK declaration, attracting those who subscribe to similar experimentation while weeding out others who are scared to err on the wrong side of fashion. In fact Monga influenced her flatmate to join the tabi tribe. “They felt super out there to me at first but I love how whimsical tabis can look,” says Udisha Madan, 27, who has just ordered her split-toe shoes. Most people will agree, the hoof lookalikes do not evoke love at first sight. Just like other great works of art—Lena Dunham’s Another factor, I suspect, that makes the design covetable is how gatekept it continues to be. In all honesty, even at its peak, the split-toe style will never become as popular as Docs, Birks or Crocs. However, that is also the point. The moment the controversial shoe wholly sinks into the mainstream, it will lose its appeal or intrigue. No one is going to ask you why you’re wearing horse hooves if everyone is wearing horse hooves.

article_title: Archival fashion was everywhere in 2025
sub_title: Archival fashion became one of the most visible styling choices, shaped by nostalgia and an increasingly crowded trend landscape
article_content: Fashion has always loved a comeback story, but lately, it has become more of a headline-maker. Archival fashion looks get social media traction, headlines and conversation, whether it’s a decades-old gown resurfacing on a red carpet or a vintage silhouette reworked through a contemporary lens. This return to the past reads as aesthetic, emotional and commercial. The current cultural instability, coupled with economic jitters and the exhaustion of the hyper-digital world that we live in has amplified the effect of the nostalgic cycle on fashion. When the present doesn’t meet our emotional needs, we look back, often with rose-tinted glasses. Every era had its own distinct fashion zeitgeist, from Y2K maximalism to the ‘90s grunge and hip-hop, and the preppy style of the ‘80s. Today’s landscape, by contrast, feels fragmented with the chaos of microtrends and overconsumption. In a market flooded with duplicates and lookalikes, vintage fashion reads as more authentic, proof of taste, effort and discernment. It offers a way to stand apart from an algorithm built on sameness. “Fashion wasn’t safe, and collections weren’t designed primarily around sales projections. That freedom produced work that still resonates today in a way that much of today’s more cautious fashion doesn’t,” says Allia Al Rufai, fashion stylist and consultant. Fashion has the capacity to shape culture in ways that extend far beyond the runway. Certain garments have become cultural markers, referenced and remembered decades later because they captured a moment with emotional force. That kind of resonance takes time, experimentation and, often, the willingness to fail. Today, the balance between artistry and business is often off-kilter. Creativity is expected to move at the speed of commerce, leaving little room for evolution. “Fashion cycles are much faster, critiques are immediate, and new creatives at heritage houses aren’t allowed enough time to experiment. They’re constantly compared to their predecessors, even before their vision has fully formed,” says SJ Singh, a fashion and culture analyst. Although designers across the world continue to push boundaries, the broader mood has changed. Iconicity rarely happens overnight. For something to become iconic, there has to be room for error and growth, a window that for some has narrowed significantly under the pressure of social media. When celebrities step out in carefully chosen pieces from a designer’s past, the response is immediate. These looks arrive with a built-in narrative, a recognisable image and a sense of intentionality that cuts through the noise. Archival dressing becomes cultural shorthand, signalling discernment rather than trend-chasing. It’s also why these moments travel so effectively. They encourage research and recognition, making it a conversation rather than a disposable moment. The resurgence of archival fashion today can feel like a retreat but perhaps is also a response to a present shaped by metrics and viral marketing. Fashion was never meant to exist solely for algorithms or rapid consumption. At its most powerful, it has been culturally tied, emotionally resonant and allowed the time to breathe. If archival fashion feels newly compelling now, it may be because it carries traces of that slower rhythm, one we are still learning how to recover.

Engagement rings became shorthand for status, a taxonomy of size, clarity and budget. “But the next generation is rejecting that logic,” says Malaika Crawford. Taste, not scale, is the new luxury, even when the stones themselves are large.

Instead of a simple shank-plus-stone formula, designers are exploring softened signets, undulating curves, melted textures, and forms that reference early modernist jewelry. “The trend right now is softer, smoother rather than sharp or geometric,” says Simpkins, whose bespoke work increasingly features signet-inspired silhouettes with “melty, imperfect texture.” Rooted in hand-engraved symbolism, Dyne shows a growing interest in tactile surfaces: brushed gold signaling a move away from high-polish gold. article_title: Karisma Kapoor’s beige Ritu Kumar anarkali relies on the power of construction
sub_title: Intricate threadwork elevates her suit set
article_content: For a recent outing, Karisma Kapoor opted for a beige kurta set from Ritu Kumar, which at a cursory glance seems pared-down but on a closer look, it’s intricate and commanding. The look’s neutral palette serves as a reminder that impact does not always rely on colour saturation. The silhouette is classic anarkali, but it is reimagined with a slightly jacket-style construction. Ritu Kumar’s beige Begum suit set unfolds with a thoughtful balance of heritage and ease. Crafted in Chanderi silk, the anarkali is structured at the bodice, where fine embroidery traces the form flowing into the fluid, flared skirt. The silhouette moves with grace, while a complementary tulle dupatta adds a diaphanous layer of lightness. Together, the elements create a look that feels ceremonial yet wearable. The embroidery deserves a special mention. Executed in resham threads, its colours draw from autumnal hues, including muted ambers, soft olives and burnished golds, and are shaped into delicate florals and foliage. A scooped back introduces a subtle sensuality and a counterpoint to the otherwise modest ensemble. Central to the outfit’s appeal is its fabric. Chanderi, often described by local artisans as “booni hui hawa” or woven air, is prized for its breathability and feather-light feel. Its ability to remain airy through humidity and transitional weather makes it ideal for Indian festivities that stretch across monsoon, autumn and winter. Long celebrated for its delicate transparency and understated lustre, Chanderi brings comfort to the forefront without sacrificing refinement. Kapoor’s beauty look completes the narrative with her signature makeup. Coppery smoky eyes paired with nude lips that keep the focus on the ensemble. She left her hair open and styled with soft curls and gentle braids at the crown. She accessorised with a gold necklace, drop earrings and bracelets from Kalyan Jewellers. From the makeup to the anarkali, it is the kind of look that will transcend seasons and occasions, making a compelling case for year-long dressing that feels festive without being fleeting.

article_content: If you want proof that a single colour can carry a whole fashion look, Alaya F’s oxblood gown does it. The look is about clean lines, strategic cut-outs and a silhouette that keeps your eye moving, rather than drowning you in detail. She wears a deep V-neck gown by C.Dam with cutaway shoulders and long glove sleeves that extend the arm into one uninterrupted line. The bodice sits close and sleek, then breaks at the hip with an asymmetric drape that reads like a folded panel, adding shape and movement before the skirt drops straight to the floor. The styling stays tight with a diamond collar necklace that sits high on the neck, repeating the gown’s geometry, with small studs to keep the focus on the neckline and shoulder line. Hair is worn down with a centre part and smooth, glossy lengths that match the dress’s clean finish. Even, luminous skin, softly defined eyes with liner and lashes, and a neutral nude lip that lets the gown’s colour stay in charge. “Alaya's cherry red ensemble is the perfect color for the festive season, her torque neckpiece steals the show. The space that the torque shape reveals creates intrigue, there are many such neckpiece shapes with stones and beads. Rethink this in a contemporary bohemian look. Work with a burgundy strapless top or tank and pair that with a ruffled asymmetrical chiffon skirt. Pair this with a bandana, a bangle stack and some thonged sandals to complete the look,” says Vogue India fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

article_title: Alia Bhatt’s archival Hervé Léger dress revisits a ’90s red-carpet silhouette
sub_title: A halter-neck bodycon from Fall/Winter 1993 brings back a body-skimming language that once dominated eveningwear
article_content: Alia Bhatt’s appearance in an archival Hervé Léger dress for the Filmfare Awards draws attention to a silhouette that once defined red-carpet dressing in the early ’90s. Styled by Rhea Kapoor, Bhatt wore a black halter-neck gown from the house’s Fall/Winter 1993 collection, part of the era when Hervé Léger’s bandage construction became a red carpet favourite,  embedded in fashion culture. The dress follows a now-familiar structure from that era: a close-fitting column that traces the body from neckline to hem, paired with a halter cut that exposes the shoulders and upper back. The fabric’s engineered stretch creates a smooth, uninterrupted surface, while the scalloped neckline introduces a subtle architectural detail. A high slit breaks the line just enough to bring in movement. This kind of silhouette appeared repeatedly on red carpets throughout the ’90s with figures like Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell and Sharon Stone often wearing similarly pared-back, body-skimming gowns. Bhatt’s styling keeps the emphasis clear. Her hair is swept back into a loose updo, leaving the neckline unobstructed. Jewellery is limited to a diamond choker and small studs. Her eye look by makeup artist Puneet B Saini is built in layers of warm browns and muted rose shimmer diffused across the lids. Skin is evened out to a satin finish, with warmth concentrated at the cheeks rather than a high-gloss highlight moment. The lips sit firmly in neutral territory, a softly contoured nude that keeps the focus upward. “Strip it back and let the dress do the talking. Lose the choker and swap it for nothing at all, bare skin feels more modern here. Loosen the hair in an almost undone way. Finish with simple black heels and a classic red lip,” says Vogue India fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

article_title: Gabriela Hearst on her arrival in India and the future of conscious fashion
sub_title: “I don’t want to contribute to more disconnection between nature and our species”
article_content: “I’ve always been conscious of what’s happening to our environment,” says Gabriela Hearst. “And I say ‘environment’ because the Earth will be fine without us. Without an environment we can survive in, humanity cannot thrive.” Long synonymous with Born in Uruguay, Hearst grew up on her family’s ranch surrounded by horses, cattle and sheep. To her, luxury has always meant things that were thoughtfully created and built for the future. After more than a decade as a designer in New York, she launched her eponymous label in 2015. “Nobody needs another fashion brand,” she says. “We desire it, yes. When I launched Gabriela Hearst, I had a long-term vision that placed sustainability and ethical sourcing as the priority. But good intentions alone aren’t enough. The design had to be exceptional.” And exceptional design is what the brand delivered. Hearst’s ‘Nina’ bag, first released in 2016, was quick to become a cult favourite. It featured a minimalistic round pouch, almost cinched at the top, with a long structured handle. Crafted from Nappa From entirely eliminating plastic packaging to staging fashion’s first carbon-neutral runway show in Spring/Summer 2020, Gabriela Hearst (the brand and the designer) has set benchmarks for sustainable luxury. A member of the board of trustees of Save the Children, Hearst has repeatedly donated proceeds from her stores to the organisation, supporting their relief efforts across the globe. Even during the designer's tenure at Chloé (December 2020–September 2023), the house became the first European luxury brand to earn B Corp certification. Below, Vogue India speaks to Gabriela Hearst about her philosophy, her practice and the story behind the Nina bag. I don’t want any polymers, petroleum or plastic even in our shoe soles. With But the bigger issue—not just for fashion, but for every industry—is energy. Until we reduce our dependence on fossil fuels, we’re in a tight spot. The good news is that new, abundant energy sources are coming down the pipeline, like fusion. We’re not going to consume less energy, and expecting developing nations to do without infrastructure or hospitals isn’t fair; that’s climate injustice. The biggest challenge, ultimately, is energy.

article_title: Karisma Kapoor’s black-and-silver EKA dress reframes linen zari for festive dressing
sub_title: A tiered dress and matching jacket highlight handloom linen from Bhagalpur, finished with zardozi embroidery and scalloped trims
article_content: Textiles make a dress, and sometimes, they make a memorable sartorial moment. Karisma Kapoor’s recent appearance in a black-and-silver EKA dress proves exactly that. With her ensemble, handwoven Called ‘Ophelia’, the tiered silhouette falls from the shoulder to hem and pintucks define its yoke. A scalloped organza trim lends an air of delicacy, while hand-embroidered zardozi borders on the hem and neckline bring a festive richness. Designer Rina Singh of EKA frames the ensemble in an artisanal narrative, “Karisma is wearing handwoven linen zari metallic stripes from the Festive ‘25 collection. The weavers are based in Bhagalpur. We have worked with these weavers since the inception of the brand 15 years ago. They are masters in handloom tussar, linen and cotton weaves. The silhouette is form-friendly and easy fit, embellished with zardozi embroidery.” Paired with the dress is the Celian jacket. A short striped Kapoor kept the styling contemporary too, with a sleek ponytail, softly smoky eyes and a muted mauve lip to complement the metallic palette. The unexpected hero is a vintage Chanel brooch pinned to her lapel, an accent that reinstates the cross-cultural dialogue. A black calfskin quilted medallion flap bag from the luxury label rounded off her accessory look. The wearability of the textile and the versatility of the silhouette make her look especially compelling for a destination wedding wardrobe. Lightweight yet opulent, linen zari thrives in tropical climates. It’s festive without being season-bound, making it an investment piece that works as seamlessly for an intimate mehendi in Goa as it does for a cocktail in Jaipur.

article_title: Janhvi Kapoor’s ivory kalidar kurta set celebrates varied craftsmanship techniques, textiles and textures
sub_title: Her Mayyur Girotra outfit took 845 man hours to complete
article_content: For a recent outing, Janhvi Kapoor opted for a kalidar kurta set by Mayyur Girotra. Despite its ivory palette, the impact of her ensemble is anything but vanilla. The outfit relies on the effortlessness of mulmul, a fabric prized in India for its breathability and softness, especially during the country’s long festive season. “Janhvi Kapoor wears Mayyur Girotra’s signature ivory mulmul kalidar that is detailed with meticulous zardozi and tilla embroidery and paired with handwoven Jamdani pyjamas,” the designer shares, setting the stage for a deep dive into the garment’s layered artistry. The kalidar, with its gentle flare and fall, became a canvas for intricately embroidered motifs of peacock, florals and foliage that lends the outfit its heirloom-worthy character. “My objective is to always create pieces that translate into heirlooms that speak about the past in the present and are here to stay for the future. And this look takes you back in time. It took 845 man hours for the look to come to life,” Girotra adds. What truly sets the look apart is the mélange of textiles, techniques and textures. “The ivory mulmul and Jamdani set is completed with an ash grey handwoven dupatta featuring classic Kanchipuram borders and rich zardozi accents, a celebration of Indian textile artistry.” The result is an outfit that brings together the finesse of Jamdani, the sheen of Kanchipuram and the delicacy of mulmul in one versatile set. The back is cut into an elegant open curve, adding a sensual counterpoint to the otherwise modest silhouette. The actor’s styling was in tandem with the nostalgic approach she aimed for. She accessorised with a Victorian-inspired ornate necklace, drop earrings and kada by Amrapali Jewels along with a ring by Golecha’s Jewels. A pair of juttis from Elements By Radhika Gupta and a silver bag by Motifs By Surabhi Didwania completed her look. Her beauty look, too, stayed true to quiet glamour, featuring sleek, centre-parted hair pulled into a polished bun. Smoky bronze lids, kohl-defined eyes and a soft nude lip completed the mood of classic, camera-ready elegance. Glamorous without overwhelming in weight or embellishment, Kapoor’s look proves that celebratory dressing in tropical climes like India can be pretty and practical.

The tree and floral motifs were designed to reflect harmony and peaceful coexistence with nature, in line with our Rewild initiative,” she notes. Each motif was drawn exclusively for the collection, hand-illustrated to evoke an emotional connection rather than merely adorn the garment. “The print is not just visually expressive but carries a sense of meaning and connection,” she reinstates. The set’s embroidery, too, is dreamed up to resonate with destination-wedding dressing. “The ensemble features intricate cord embroidery with subtle sequin detailing. It brings depth and light to the silk, while keeping the overall mood calm, refined and timeless.” The three-piece structure, comprising a cropped skirt, bralette and gilet, makes a compelling case for hands-free celebration. With no dupatta to manage and a flattering, effortless fall, it’s the kind of silhouette that invites dancing, mingling and moving through a wedding weekend with ease. “A detail we hold close are the concealed pockets in our outfits,” Dongre adds. “They offer comfort and ease without interrupting the elegance of the silhouette, reinforcing the idea that craftsmanship and functionality can coexist beautifully.” The set, which came to life over nearly 60 days of patient hand-embroidery, is “a reminder that true luxury is shaped by time, intention and craftsmanship.” A pair of ruby and diamond encrusted earrings and ring by Amrapali Jewels. For footwear, she kept it comfy with Fizzy Goblet mules adorned with 3D gold leaves along with nakashi and patti work. article_title: The Pantone colour of the year is Cloud Dancer, a natural white
sub_title: “It’s about expressing our aspiration for a future free from toxicity and excess”
article_content: Since 1999, Pantone has been selecting a colour that will characterise the culture of the year ahead. “We wanted to highlight to our audience how what is taking place in our global culture is expressed and reflected through the language of colour,” Laurie Pressman, Vice President of the Pantone Colour Institute, “We talk about, is it an evolution or a seismic shift?” Pressman adds on a call to discuss 2026’s Pantone colour of the year selection with The relief will come in the form of a shade they’ve dubbed Cloud Dancer, “a lofty white that reads like a breath of fresh air and is imbued with a feeling of serenity,” as Lee Eisman, Pantone’s executive director, describes it. “It’s about expressing our aspiration for a future free from toxicity and excess. Cloud Dancer evolves our desire for contentment and harmony and the feeling of peace, unity, and cohesiveness.” Pressman adds, “It’s not a stark white, it’s specifically a natural shade of white.” It’s an unexpected choice. Given the current political and cultural climate, declaring a shade of white the colour of the year is a bold statement. At the same time, observing the world around us—which is first and foremost what the Institute does—it’s almost as if there were no other possible options. Indeed, we are all searching for purity; we just have such different ideas of how to go about it. Aesthetically speaking, white it is a colour that does not disturb, does not rock the boat, a colour easily found in everything around us: in cars, in architecture, in furniture and interiors, even in food, and certainly in fashion where it is a “classic,” that “never goes out of style,” and a “wardrobe essential.” White simultaneously hints at futuristic sensibilities—minimal, stark, clean—and at traditional ones—“It’s a nice day for a white wedding,” “When we went down this path, we felt very strongly about encouraging creativity, encouraging you to use your imagination and bring this [color] in a way that suits who you are and how you want others to see you and how you want to feel,” Pressman concluded. “It’s self-expression.” Below, the best examples of the Pantone colour of the year, Cloud Dancer-white, on the spring 2026 runways.

article_title: Ara Pret by Kulsum Shadab Wahab is pioneering purpose-led fashion

article_content: “So many acid-attack survivors have been made to feel invisible, so giving them that light, giving them that platform was very important to me,” says Kulsum Shadab Wahab, philanthropist and founder of Ara Lumiere and Ara Pret. Through her brands, she’s worked to create spaces where these survivors can rebuild their confidence, express themselves through creativity and rediscover a sense of self-worth. Her impact, within the fashion industry and outside of it, also lead to her appointment as the first Indian Ambassador for Women’s Empowerment by the Camera Nazionale della Moda Italiana (Italian Fashion Council). Launched in 2019, Ara Lumiere has earned global recognition for its handcrafted Building on Ara Lumiere’s success, Shadab Wahab launched Ara Pret in August of this year, a ready-to-wear label that focuses on affordability, everyday design and empowerment. Each piece is ethically crafted and rooted in the stories of the women it supports. With its clean silhouettes and timeless appeal, Ara Pret marks a new chapter in Indian fashion—purpose-led prêt, where style and social change go hand in hand. Below, the philanthropist opens up about how she got started, the vision behind her brands and the moments that make it all worthwhile.

article_title: Sonam Kapoor makes a case for Tangkhul craft in an EAST set

article_content: Sonam Kapoor rarely misses a chance to champion Indian craft, and this time, she turned to Manipur’s EAST for the Architectural Digest dinner hosted at her Mumbai home. The actor slipped into the label’s Tangkhul Kashan-inspired ĀKHA set from the Patron Collection. “This collection stands as a tribute to every client who has been part of our journey and helped sustain our craft,” says designer Easternlight Zimik. It’s the same body of work he recently showcased in Seoul, handloom-rooted in Tangkhul Naga identity and reinterpreted through a deeply personal design language. The ĀKHA look leaned into the language of Tangkhul textiles with minimal interference: a wrap-style upper layer tied at the back, worn over a black collared shirt and paired with a matching skirt or kashan, its monochrome palette and clean lines keeping the focus firmly on the craft. “ĀKHA—meaning first number in our dialect—marks the opening look of the Patrons Collection,” Zimik shares. The textile, handwoven on the traditional loin loom, draws from the essence of four of EAST’s previous collections, “weaving together our most beloved pieces into one unified creation,” he adds. The Kashan traditions came through in its linear motifs, ribbed panels and tasselled ends, each rooted in Tangkhul weaving, where shifts in line, density and rhythm carry cultural meaning. For this iteration, Zimik notes that the studio worked with the rich tonalities of autumn, “intertwining two distinct patterns, one from our RASI series that reimagines our land’s night sky in constellation-like dots and another that echoes the enduring canopy of trees, the silent guardians of our homeland.” Finished with grand, flowing fringes, the look becomes “a celebration of craft, lineage, and cultural memory.” Her jewellery from Zoya added metallic polish: a sleek gold choker inlaid with tiny Her beauty look stayed minimal with centre-parted hair worn down, smoky eyes and barely-there matte skin, keeping the focus on the craft-forward silhouette. “The Tangkhul Kashan inspired set is already a statement in and of itself. Go heavier on the metal jewellery to amplify the look; think oversized and oxidised molten metal jewellery,” says Vogue India fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

article_title: How to make sheer dresses work off the red carpet
sub_title: From smart layering to texture play, here’s how to bring sheer into your wardrobe
article_content: Sheer dresses have always been a fashion favourite. But it has mostly lived in the red-carpet ecosystem. Rihanna in Adam Selman? Iconic. Also the kind of dress you’d never wear outside a chauffeured car. Out of journalistic curiosity, I once asked my mother how she’d style a sheer dress. The look she gave me could have stripped paint off the walls and possibly summoned a That reaction reminded me how sheer dresses (or any garment, really), despite never being new to India, still make people clutch imaginary pearls. “Sheer dressing in India has always carried an interesting duality, it’s both traditional and modern. If we think about it, sheer elements have long existed in Indian clothing through fabrics like Sheer is stunning on the carpet, but can it survive real pavement? After all, few things in fashion are as intimidating to wear in real life, maybe, barring Margiela Tabi shoes. “Celebrities on the red carpet have entire teams ensuring everything stays perfectly in place, but for everyday wear, you want to feel secure and comfortable while still keeping the look interesting,” reminds Sandeep Tupili, founder and creative director at Maison Tai. “Sheer can sound intimidating at first, but confidence is everything. The trick is to highlight the areas you feel comfortable showing, that way, the sheer detail feels intentional, elegant, and never awkward,” suggests Tupili. Rather than diving head-first (or body-first) into the trend, Nefertari Joshi, founder of Nef’s Finds, recommends beginning gently. “Play with fabric textures like lace, georgette, crochet or embroidery and let the sheerness become part of your personal style narrative rather than a bold experiment. You can even start with pieces that already play with a mix of sheerness so it’s more wearable.” It’s important to let sheer dresses have their moment. Joshi adds that the most common mistake is trying to do everything at once. “They tend to either over-layer, losing the delicacy that makes sheer fabrics so special, or under-layer, which can feel accidental rather than intentional.” “I love pairing sheer with a corset, clipping the sheer layer to the corset instantly adds structure and elegance. Try gathering or crunching the sheer slightly for extra visual interest, and if you’re feeling bold, layer it over a semi-sheer corset for a daring yet refined look,” advises Tupili. In case you are planning your next vacation, Joshi recommends Sheer dresses over bikini sets or bralets. “It really enhances the figure and is perfect for vacation dressing.” And for everyday elegance? “Tailored blazers or waistcoats instantly add sharpness — pair a sheer blouse with wide-leg trousers and a blazer or waistcoat for an understated power look,” says Joshi. “A crisp white shirt under a sheer dress really balances androgyny with an otherwise feminine silhouette." “There’s something so poetic about sheer fabrics being paired with delicate lace detailing. The sheerness allows the lace to truly stand out, creating a play of texture that feels feminine yet understated,” says Jajodia. But in a country where the weather is always plotting against you, layering takes strategy. “Balancing layers in sheer dressing is about creating depth without overheating. Pair sheer overlays with fitted inner slips or camisoles in breathable fabrics like cotton, silk, or modal. Soft, pastel colours and light fabrics naturally help keep the look airy and elegant,” says Jajodia. This year belonged to sheer, from Margot Robbie’s Armani Privé moment to Madison Beer at the Grammys 2025. And maybe it can be yours too, minus the red carpets and minus the oopsies.

article_title: The lace-trim dress has become the ultimate cool-girl staple
sub_title: The lace-trim dress has lasted decades (and yes, we have receipts)
article_content: Scroll through a model’s Instagram or any set of paparazzi shots, and you will spot a lace-trim dress soon enough. A scalloped hem peeking from under a During a The lingerie-as-outerwear idea continues to resurface, each time in a fresh guise. Kaia Gerber favours nineties bias cuts; Bella Hadid opts for halters and polka dots, a quiet nod to nonchalance. After the polished austerity of quiet luxury and the exuberance of the Y2K revival, fashion has found a middle ground: tactile, emotional, familiar. These pieces feel personal, like something you might have discovered in your mother’s wardrobe or at a Henrietta Rix, co-founder of RIXO, a British label specialising in lace-trimmed silhouettes, explains, “There is a clear link to the ’90s supermodel aesthetic — think Kate Moss in silk slips — that still influences how women dress today. Contrasts work best: a delicate lace edge against a bold print or rich colour. Placement matters; framing the neckline or hem draws the eye and enhances femininity without tipping into overt sweetness. And craftsmanship matters too — quality lace makes all the difference.” You know the formula by now: Then come the pop girls: Olivia Rodrigo pairs hers with cowboy boots, Sabrina Carpenter goes butter-yellow, Gracie Abrams wears them on tour, and Kacey Musgraves collaborated with Reformation on lace–trimmed pieces. Rix sums it up: “The lace-trim silhouette has a sensuality, undone in the best possible way. You can wear it and look composed without seeming over-styled. For daytime, I love grounding it with something unexpected, a chunky knit or trainers. Evening is about letting the dress shine: a delicate heel, some vintage-inspired jewellery, maybe a silk scarf.” Meghna Goyal, the founder of Summer Away, adds: “By day, a long lace-trim tunic layered over a sweater or T-shirt, paired with trousers and edgy accessories, feels modern. By night, a silk slip under a structured blazer or co-ord set makes for a polished finish.” Lace trims have been everywhere lately — Chloé, Carolina Herrera, Dries Van Noten, Fendi, Alberta Ferretti, Blumarine, Shiatzy Chen and Saint Laurent. From minis to asymmetric midis, slips to sweeping gowns. Goyal notes, “These dresses have dominated runways for seasons. What makes them stand out now is how they are layered with unconventional, edgy pieces. The mix gives each outfit a distinct energy. For models and pop stars, it’s a piece that moves from day to night, cafe to stage, always looking intentional even when thrown on last minute.” And the new guard is carrying the torch. SIR, Dôen, Realisation Par, Zimmermann, Charo Ruiz, Self Portrait, For Love & Lemons, Sandro, Retrofete, and VRG GRL are giving lace a modern spin — less prim, more personality. Lace-trim dresses keep coming back because they are more than just pretty. A masterclass in contradiction made wearable — sweet but sly, soft but self–assured. Between shows or on a humid Sunday, a lace midi makes it look like you just woke up interesting. And when Cox joked about the number, “It’s probably gone in and out of style four times,” Aniston simply said, “It will always be in style.” She was right.

article_title: Why are men with nose piercings hotter?
sub_title: It’s no longer about rebellion but about comfort, confidence and cultural reconnection
article_content: Of the few things my corner of the internet unanimously agrees on, it’s this: Zayn Malik is probably the hottest man alive. Hotter, since he got a nose The current poster boy for men with nose piercings follows in the dashing footsteps of Tupac Shakur and Lenny Kravitz, the few male celebrities bold enough to get a nose piercing. But the risk (and pain, described as a sharp pinch) pays off. “Men with no nose piercing, what is stopping you from simply piercing your nose? get to it thanks,” reads another tweet with over 2,000 likes. I tap on the heart button. Luckily for me, India has historically celebrated bejewelled piercings as a form of body modification. “Jewellery was a marker of celebration, identity and status,” notes In 1995, the first strains of this revival came from the unlikeliest of sources: Akshay Kumar, in a magazine photoshoot, pulling off a nose chain. Then Ranveer Singh followed in 2016. Aamir Khan’s 2017 nose stud—in addition to his pierced ears—only adds to what the internet fondly refers to as his ‘divorced lesbian’ look. Now, from social media’s favourite DILF Kanan Gill to director Bijoy Shetty, it feels like every cool guy is lining up to puncture their nostrils and septums. Shetty confesses he got his nose pierced seven years ago, at the age of 20, only because his sisters had too. “They were just badasses and people in my family were scared of them. I wanted to emulate that energy and feel more confident,” he shares. “Women are definitely still a majority but men have also started checking the option, especially post Covid,” says professional piercer and tattoo artist My group chat heartily supports this uptick, as do the many women who slide into my DMs when I put up an Instagram story asking to connect with men who have pierced noses. “Send him my way once you’re done with journalistic work,” a friend quips. I ask them: What makes men with nose piercings so irresistible? “It shows comfort in their own masculinity,” one replies on the group chat. “That they’re not afraid to be a little feminine,” another adds. In 2007, On that tweet asking what’s stopping men from getting their noses pierced, a popular response from a man reads, “Because I’m not gay.” Shetty finds that while most people admire his facial piercings, they also make him a target for harassment. “In public transport, I’ve had men approach me, touch me inappropriately, call me names. College was also difficult because random boys would say weirdly homophobic things,” he admits. “My family says I look like a cow because of my septum ring,” confesses 30-year-old Nikhil Poddar, an artist based in Bengaluru, “Sometimes older people in my village ask if I’m a girl because they’re only used to seeing women with septum piercings.” 22-year-old Delhi-based musician Farookh got one to dispute this very perception. “I’d wanted to get a nose piercing since 10th grade but my conservative Catholic school didn’t allow it,” he says. “But also, as someone who makes hip hop music, I wanted to challenge the ingrained idea of hypermasculinity that people often associate with this genre.” Of course, I reckon #notallmen can pull one off. But for some, the humble nose piercing has been life-changing. For sports commentator Pulasta Dhar, it was a nose piercing that sealed the deal with his then-Hinge match, now-wife Sakshi Rawte-Dhar. “She had two piercings on both sides of her nose, so when we matched on Hinge, my first message was something along the lines of ‘Btw, I have a nose piercing, so if this works out, I’m going to steal all your nose jewellery.’ Cut to a few months later and she’s stealing all of my nose jewellery every day.” To the men who are still on the fence: a Hinge photo update might be overdue.

article_title: Inside real weddings: A photographer’s guide to capturing intimate celebrations
sub_title: From shared laughter to candid, intimate moments, Fourfold Pictures brings every wedding emotion to life behind the lens
article_content: Couples are reclaiming their wedding stories and prioritising emotion and authenticity over perfection. Rather than putting on a spectacle, the focus is on intimate and meaningful interactions with loved ones, with photographs becoming the ultimate keepsakes. That’s why picking the right wedding photographer is an essential part of planning your big day. Mumbai-based wedding photographer duo Gaurav and Priyanka Shukla came together to capture candid memories. Co-founders of Fourfold Pictures, they have a knack for anticipating pivotal moments, with honesty in storytelling being paramount to their work. Over time, Gaurav and Priyanka have built a brand that attracts couples seeking intention, aesthetic depth, and a distinct visual identity. Notably, A-listers such as actors Parineeti Chopra and Aadar Jain, singer Prakriti Kakar, and content creator Aaliyah Kashyap, among others, are part of their repertoire. While editorial sophistication defines their portfolio, the heart of Fourfold Pictures is rooted in human connection. From intimate ceremonies to grand celebrations, the brand is dedicated to creating enduring visual stories—memories couples can revisit for years to come. The photographers share their insights on capturing intimate nuptials, understanding what modern couples value most, and remembering what truly matters once the camera starts rolling. “We begin by understanding emotion before aesthetics,” says the duo. Every wedding starts with an internal mood board—light, texture, rhythm, restraint. The final gallery is edited with a fashion sensibility and a storyteller’s heart: timeless, not trend-led. Intimate weddings allow for emotional closeness. With fewer people, the energy shifts inward. The focus shifts from spectacle to presence, nuance, and genuine human connection. Each wedding has its own visual language. Sometimes the destination exists as a subtle backdrop; other times it becomes a character within the story. “We let the location influence colour, light, and mood—never overpowering the couple themselves,” mentions the duo. Intimacy creates space for stillness. “We look for the moments in between moments—glances, silences, and gentle gestures. Those details often carry the deepest emotion,” the duo reflects. Trust comes with intention and discretion. “We work unobtrusively, allowing couples to remain fully present. When they feel unobserved, authenticity emerges naturally,” shares the duo. Culture shapes rhythm and expression. “We respond by adapting my pace and framing—honouring tradition while maintaining an editorial lens that feels contemporary and refined,” says the duo. Think beyond simply capturing moments. Focus on how you want the day to feel. When emotion leads, the images naturally become aesthetically meaningful. Intimate weddings are often mistaken for being simpler, but in reality, they’re emotionally layered and visually sophisticated. They allow for more intentional storytelling, editorial-style portraits, and visionary experiences that are often harder to achieve in larger celebrations. “A quiet pause shared between the couple, away from the ceremony and guests. No performance—just presence. These are the moments that linger long after the wedding ends,” Gaurav concludes.

article_title: This Delhi couple’s story is the perfect example of the invisible string theory
sub_title: How Pavani Nagpal and Karan Chhabra’s parallel lives, chance meeting and artistic wedding came together in a story of serendipity
article_content: Fate works in mysterious ways, bringing together two people who are meant to be with each other. East Asian folklore refers to this phenomenon as the ‘red thread of fate’ or, as popular culture describes it, the invisible string theory. A large part of content today, from books to movies, is inspired by this whimsical bit of folklore. It depicts two people crossing paths through time and distance, never quite pausing, until one destined moment of clarity (a meet-cute, for all you rom-com enthusiasts) brings them together. Bringing this fictional belief to life is the story of Pavani Nagpal and Karan Chhabra. Nagpal, a visual artist, and Chhabra, a tech professional, studied in the same school and later also went to the same university, walking the corridors and complaining about their teachers. But their paths never crossed. Years passed and Nagpal founded her own art studio, Pavsarts Art Studio, while Chhabra became the CEO of Acefone, a business communications company. Until they finally met in what would seem like a scene right out of a romantic movie, at a party, where Nagpal accidentally spilled a drink on Chhabra. Chhabra, like the ever-charming male lead, joked that he deserved a discount on one of Nagpal’s paintings. “And that single moment changed everything,” the visual artist tells us. Fate had set the dice rolling. The couple began dating, got engaged and were married, all within a year. Their wedding celebrations were a blend of art, heritage, couture and the magic of two people finding their way to each other. Unfolding slowly over a month, each celebration reflected a different emotion, from devotion to joy. Starting the wedding ceremonies on an auspicious note, the couple organised a mata ki chowki. Bathed in shades of red and enhanced by two of the bride’s paintings, the decor made the space look like a film set. Matching the Indian classical sensibilities, the bride wore a Sabyasachi ensemble while the groom adorned a custom lakhnawi kurta set. A few weeks after that, the pair got engaged in a joyous ceremony filled with song, dance and laughter. The venue was decorated elegantly, inspired by a painting Nagpal had made just before meeting Chhabra. “My painting manifested him in my life,” the bride exclaimed. She donned another beautiful Sabyasachi outfit for the ceremony while the groom complemented her in a timeless Rohit Bal outfit. The mehendi was a deeply personal affair for Nagpal, as she hosted it at Pavsarts Art Studio, her own space, surrounded by colours, canvases and her work. “It felt like my journey as an artist and my journey in love were coming together in the same space,” she said. Wearing Anamika Khanna and Manish Malhotra, the bride and groom fit into the venue just right, looking like they’d walked straight out of one of Nagpal’s paintings. The mehendi night was followed by a floral haldi morning at The Leela Palace, Chanakyapuri. The couple and their wedding guests played phoolon ki haldi, a ritual where, along with the traditional turmeric, fragrant flowers are also used. A highlight of the event was when the usually calm and composed Chhabra surprised everyone with an energetic performance. The bride looked radiant in a bright pink Shobhika Bhandari saree while the groom matched her, wearing a pastel pink Rohit Bal ensemble. The bright and cold morning of November eight marked the couple’s wedding day. It was a traditional and emotional celebration, less about spectacle and more about the couple beginning their new life together. In royal Sabyasachi and Rohit Bal ensembles, the couple looked radiant with happiness and love, surrounded by near and dear ones. What began as parallel lives eventually became a shared one, guided by timing, chance and perhaps a little bit of destiny. Two people, once strangers walking the same corridors, were unknowingly tethered by an invisible string, until fate finally pulled them together into a moment and led them to a lifetime of companionship.

article_title: “I wear it on my middle finger”: Inside the booming market for divorce rings
sub_title: “I’m complimented on it surprisingly often, which always makes me smile. Not because of what it represents to anyone else, but because it reminds me that I trusted myself when it mattered"
article_content: Peer through the window of Annoushka Ducas’s London boutique in the evening, and you might spy women poring over diamonds and sipping champagne. But they aren’t congregating to peruse engagement rings or push presents, they’re toasting the signing of Ducas is just one of a host of jewellers responding to the growing appetite for divorce rings, fuelled in part by the sizeable jewels sported by A-listers after they’ve signed on the dotted line to singledom. Take Emily Ratajkowski, who back in March 2024, commemorated her divorce from her husband of two years, Sebastian Bear-McClard, with two platinum and 18-carat rings designed by Alison Lou, which incorporated the pear-shaped and princess-cut diamonds from her In January, original power stylist and newly inaugurated Real Housewife Rachel Zoe marked her split from her husband of over 20 years, Rodger Berman, with a jaw-dropping three-stone divorce ring designed by Ring Concierge, which transformed the huge cushion-cut diamond of her halo engagement ring. Elsewhere, celebrity dermatologist Barbara Sturm commissioned her Jessica McCormack divorce ring before her separation from husband Adam Waldman had even been finalised. “Once you’ve made the decision, you’re already there, even if the paperwork isn’t through,” she says. Posting the final creation on Instagram in October 2025–a chunky twisted gold ring with a pear-shaped diamond–she namechecked EmRata as her inspiration. Unsurprisingly, East London jeweller Rachel Boston–who says she has been working on divorce ring commissions for the last four years–has found her clients clamouring for bespoke designs that look anything but traditionally “bridal”. “Clients are gravitating towards pieces that feel more grounded and everyday, like chunky bands, sculptural settings, and designs that can be worn as part of a daily uniform,” she explains. “Signet style rings and wide gold bands are popular.” Chelsea-based jeweller Jessie Thomas agrees. “We see a lot of chunky yellow and white gold pieces, with heavy settings and large stones.” Tania and Dima Nawbar, of fourth-generation Beirut-based jeweller Atelier Nawbar, also note the same affinity for the oversized. A recent divorce ring commission saw the central diamond and halo stones from a wedding and engagement ring transformed into a pebble-like cocktail ring, shimmering with bezel-set diamonds. “I hadn’t expected how often I’d absently reach for my wedding rings without thinking, or how their absence would become an unwanted reminder of the struggle I was going through,” says 32-year-old Madeleine Phillips. The East Sussex-based marketing director commissioned a divorce ring three months after her separation was finalised. “I didn’t want to repurpose my wedding or engagement rings. At that point they felt too emotionally loaded, and looking back, I’m glad I didn’t try and bring a piece of my past into the present. I wanted something symbolic, that felt very intentional, but it needed to be new.” Working with an online jeweller, Phillips commissioned a yellow gold ring set with baguette-cut “deliberately defiant” black diamonds. “It has 11 stones, one for each year we were together. That wasn’t something I set out to do, but once I saw it, the choice felt precise, rather than sentimental.” Phillips initially wore her divorce ring on her ring finger, before having it resized to fit her middle one. “That progression was always part of the plan I had for it, and the way the ring has evolved with me feels part of its story.” Lylie’s Eliza Walters has also noted commissions for rings designed to be worn on the middle finger, like chunky Etruscan-inspired settings, “intentionally removing any visual or symbolic association with a traditional engagement ring”. Barbara Sturm also designed her ring to sit on the middle of her hand. “But my 11-year-old daughter, Pepper, told me it looked cooler on my index finger,” she says, smiling. Twice-divorced Victoria Comstock-Kershaw, an art critic, continues to wear both of her engagement rings stacked on her ring finger. “I’ve kept wearing after the divorce, which I’m told is absolutely insane, but my logic was: I liked them enough at the time, and I continue to trust my taste in jewellery more than I trust my taste in men,” she says. At her weddings, the 27-year-old had exchanged vows with rings she already owned: choosing first a green tourmaline and silver ring gifted to her by her grandmother, and then a diamond and lilac sapphire band from a now-defunct jeweller in Burlington Arcade that was originally a 21st birthday present to her mother, who gave it to her daughter when she turned 21. “Aesthetically I find them immensely satisfying (I often get my nails done to match the first one),” she says. “Socially, they are simultaneously a good deterrent to flash at flirters (‘sorry, married!’) and a great conversation starter with anybody who compliments them (‘what do you mean your It doesn’t have to be a ring, either. Barbara Sturm repurposed two small pear-shaped diamonds from her original engagement ring into earrings, while Annoushka and Rachel Boston have had enquiries into pendant necklaces. “Divorce has a way of unsettling your sense of self. Change was going to be uncomfortable regardless, so I chose to mark it on my own terms, with a reminder of the version of me who chose decisiveness over doubt, at a point when that really mattered,” says Phillips. “Now, my ring feels more about confidence than recovery. I’m complimented on it surprisingly often, which always makes me smile. Not because of what it represents to anyone else, but because it reminds me that I trusted myself when it mattered.”
