sub_title: Andrea Kurunathan and Prem Anand Umapathy share a business, workplace and most waking hours. Here’s how planning their wedding revealed why they work so well together
article_content: For Andrea Kurunathan and Prem Anand Umapathy, love was never rushed. It unfolded slowly, shaped by friendship, shared ambition, humour and years of perseverance. Kurunathan, an aesthetic physician, and Umapathy, a civil engineer and interior designer, met through mutual friends when they were 18 and 22. They were polar opposites, and their first impressions of each other weren’t promising—no one would have guessed that the couple would go on to run a successful business together, let alone turn that partnership into a marriage that began with exchanging vows by the sea in Phuket. So how did the couple find themselves in a South Indian wedding in Thailand? Through years of friendship—supporting one another through educational endeavours, career uncertainty and major life decisions—Kurunathan fell for Umapathy’s humour and calm steadiness, while Umapathy admired her drive and clarity. Before tying the knot, the pair built a life together, navigating pressure, differences and ambition. They co-founded Luxury Derm Clinic, a luxury aesthetic clinic in Chennai, learning each other’s rhythms and accepting that being opposites did not mean being incompatible. So when it came time to plan a multi-city, deeply personal wedding, they approached it the same way they approach everything else: with intention, defined roles and very little ego. Here’s how they did it while enjoying the process of planning a wedding instead of letting it stress them out. One of the most important reasons the couple work well together is their existing partnership. It made the process of planning the wedding easier—they already knew how decisions were made, who would lead where, and when to step back. “We approached the wedding the same way we approach building our business. We have always known that we are better together than alone, and that belief shapes everything we build,” shared the bride. “We divided responsibilities instinctively, based on what each of us enjoys and does best,” Umapathy explained. The bride took charge of the aesthetics, storytelling and creative direction, while the groom supported her vision through precise execution, drawing on his technical expertise. From a floral mehendi sundowner to a traditional South Indian wedding in Phuket, (a location deeply personal to the couple) every ceremony was Kurunathan’s brainchild, brought to life through Umapathy’s engineering precision. For two people so different in temperament, disagreements were inevitable, but they rarely turned personal. “We understand each other’s strengths and give each other a lot of space. We do not step into each other’s territory unless help is needed. When it is, we show up fully. That balance is what keeps things easy between us,” said Kurunathan. There were no major disagreements, only a few light-hearted ones. Kurunathan wanted to be the loud, proud Indian bride with elaborate outfits and wedding dances, while the shy and reserved Umapathy wasn’t comfortable with all the attention. In the end, the groom surprised everyone on the dance floor and delivered a wedding speech that had guests in stitches. Kurunathan’s looks—from a blue floral Ariyali lehenga by Mrunalini Rao at the mehendi to a classic red-and-gold Kanchipuram silk saree for the wedding—were striking designer outfits. On the other hand, Umapathy chose refined, understated ensembles, staying true to himself while still complementing the bride. After watching the couple build a successful business together, their families trusted their clarity and vision. While family members played a central role in shaping the wedding, final decisions always rested with the bride and groom. “Everyone respected each other’s space, and we were all more focused on fine-tuning and shaping ideas rather than controlling them. It became a very collaborative process. It was not a wedding run for us; it was a wedding built by us, with family standing firmly behind us,” the groom explained. In the end, it’s about knowing whose vision to trust, building something together, and leaving ego out of the equation. And that, perhaps, is what made the Kurunathan-Umapathy wedding truly special.

article_title: 4 almost-brides tell us how they braved wedding season in India after their weddings were called off
sub_title: Spill the tea, but don’t be tacky
article_content: Congratulations to us all. We’re halfway through wedding season in India. We’ve braved nuptials we were invited to and reluctantly attended, as well as those we watched unfold on But, let’s admit it, the most You know the ones: the blended WhatsApp wedding group suddenly goes eerily silent. Soon enough, private chats are ablaze with gleeful/glum I-knew-its, followed by Now imagine being the unwilling heroine perched at the centre of the expensive operatic mess that is a cancelled wedding. Or its polite cousin, the indefinitely impending nuptials. And imagine enduring a These four women survived the carnage to give us a definitive ‘how to’ guide: how to prep for the chaos, how to commiserate without being cloying, how to be a girl’s girl even while dishing the dirt. It’s going to hurt to see people get married on or around your wedding day, even if you’re the one who ended things. Preparing for pain somewhat inures you against it. If you’re attending weddings around the time you were meant to be married, it’s quite likely that you’ll be the topic of conversation or even subjected to outright intrusiveness. If you can’t handle the side-eyes or gossip, don’t attend. If you do attend, don’t make a spectacle of yourself. Whatever you do, don’t be a drunken slob. There’s no moral or egotistical victory to be won by attending. I’d even recommend the high road and, if possible, let them know you won’t be there so they’re not walking on eggshells. Not everyone needs to know you did the leaving and why. If your ex feels the need to save face by making you the jilted instead of the jiltee, allow them this small grace. There might be occasions when your friends will feel like they need to defend your honour out of loyalty. Tell them exactly what and how much is okay to share, so they’re spared the mental gymnastics. If you’re the friend who has to establish that your bestie isn’t, in fact, an irredeemable villain, stick to the approved script no matter how much you’re itching to set the record straight. …but it’s not okay to be guillotined for acting in your best interests. A polite-but-firm “moving on” to change topics is perfectly acceptable when Detective Do-Gooder decides to make your business their business. Travel. Sit this wedding season out, regardless of whose wedding you’re missing. If your wedding’s been called off because you cheated, there’s no way the sordid details haven’t made the rounds. …and that none of it will be kind to you, a lot of it will reach you. When that happens, keep your crashouts (there will be many) private. When the invariable “But what the hell happened?” question rolls around, don’t lie, don’t try to justify, don’t try to play the victim. Even if you think you had reasons for cheating, keep them to yourself. “I made a mistake” is a perfectly adequate comment. Even if you’re in a relationship with them now, the wedding season is not the time to go official. Seeming too gleeful will make you come off as petty and crass. Do the decent thing and pretend to feel bad. Bitterness is aggressively unappealing at weddings, even for a bride-that-wasn’t. It might be economical, but it’s also pathetic and cartoonish. If you can’t be civil in public, don’t attend weddings together. Be very careful about what you say. Families have a way of magically resolving issues overnight (or, better still, pretending they never existed at all). They might forgive each other, but they won’t forgive you. It’s just going to make you sound pitiful and prolong the cycle of misery. “We’ll let you know when we have a date” is sufficient engagement with self-appointed town criers. Don’t run around declaring the time of death on the couple. You don’t want to be the friend who had no faith if the wedding actually gets resuscitated.

For the For their The wedding day at Marriott Lincolnshire was everything they had hoped for when they chose Chicago—open skies, calm waters, and the presence of close friends and family. The pheras took place by the lake as the light softened around them, creating a moment that was both simple and sacred. Ashima looked radiant in Varun Bahl, while Garv shone in Divyam Mehta. The celebrations wound down the next morning with a celebratory brunch, the kind where people linger because they’re not quite ready for it all to end. SDS Studio remained behind the lens throughout, capturing the celebrations with a sensitivity that matched the spirit of the weekend. “As a destination wedding photographer, I witnessed Ashima and Garv's wedding unfold in a beautifully organic way—guided by emotion, light, and movement rather than staged moments. The celebrations were captured as they naturally evolved, with editorial bridal frames introduced sparingly and with intention. The result is a visual narrative that feels raw, refined, and timeless,” reflects Sabareesh. The guest list was intentionally small, which meant every face carried a story and every exchange held meaning. Chicago, with its mix of family roots and beauty, served as the natural backdrop for a wedding that felt intimate without being small and festive without ever losing its charm. “We believe the most beautiful weddings are led by emotion rather than excess, guided by a philosophy of understated luxury. This intimate Chicago celebration was thoughtfully planned around the couple’s story, allowing their love and quiet moments to take centre stage,” reflects Sidharth Mahajan, Founder, Ómorfo Events. In the end, Ashima and Garv’s wedding wasn’t designed to dazzle. It was simply a reflection of who they are. Thoughtful. Warm. A little nostalgic. A little modern. And quietly certain of where they’re headed together.

article_title: Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding had approximately 10 lakh flowers
sub_title: We speak to Interflora India’s founder, Anuja Joshi, who played a pivotal role in beautifying Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding in Udaipur
article_content: There are weddings that trend and there are weddings that become the talk of the town. Then there are weddings where every little detail is so extravagant, so excessive, that the entire internet wants to get involved. The recent nuptials of billionaire heiress But how many flowers does it actually take to break the internet? 10 lakh flower stems and 800 florists is the floral math behind Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding. “Three rounds of floral sampling were done with the bride alone. Netra knew exactly what she wanted. The florals had to honour the sanctity of Indian culture yet be styled in a distinctly European manner,” says Anuja Joshi, founder at Interflora India. “No chrysanthemums, no carnations, no daisies and none of the typical “filler flowers” made the cut. Ranunculus featured at every event as Netra loves them.” Each colour and flower served a purpose; nothing was used just to fill space. “Inspired by ‘navratna’ (the nine cosmic jewels believed to harmonise and bless new beginnings), the wedding unfolded across six events in different palatial settings where we assigned every event its own hero flower which spoke to the bride’s taste,” Joshi added. Burgundy hydrangeas accordingly led the way to the Welcome Dinner, while the peach-and-orange fruit-inspired palette for the haldi was set against a bougainvillaea canopy. The Cirque du Soleil–inspired mehendi was a nod to one of the couple’s early dates, with deep purple alliums turning the celebration into a mini dreamscape. A Bollywood-meets-opera sangeet drifted into pink monochrome with phalaenopsis and peonies as showstoppers. The wedding ceremony bloomed with white hydrangeas while the reception closed the festivities with a pristine cloud of white phalaenopsis. For a wedding of this scale, floral emergencies are practically accounted for, except the one at Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding looked like it had stepped out of the pages of a fairytale. “All the wedding flowers that were meant to arrive three days before the wedding only landed the evening before. Picture this: thousands of fresh-cut blooms landed at the venue at 5pm, and because this was Jagmandir Island Palace, the only way to bring them in was by water. Cue boatloads and midnight sprints to pull off the early morning wedding setup in record time,” Joshi recalls. The wedding came with its own logistical ballet of flipping multiple heritage venues in impossible timelines, backstage transitions on clockwork and a 15,000sqft cold room built solely to store the flowers. While people assume viral weddings are only about the grand pieces and monumental installations, Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding achieved a sweet balance. “Grandeur isn’t in piling more things but in detailing and layering. Udaipur is not your average venue—it’s a living museum of centuries-old domes and palatial walls, so the decor should never compete with but complement the architecture,” Joshi explains. The Interflora team decked the palace walls with never-before-seen green cascades and purple delphiniums to elevate the guest walkway at City Palace’s Manek Chowk for the mehendi function. Later, for the nuptials at the Jagmandir Island Palace, the existing central dome was reimagined as the mandap, resembling a temple in the middle of a lake adorned with traditional South Indian flowers. The backdrop featured a floral-crafted Shri Yantra (a geometric symbol comprising nine interlocking triangles that are considered powerful in Hindu and Buddhist traditions), transforming the space into a site of spiritual resonance. In a land of extravagant weddings, it takes something exceptionally unique to make an Indian wedding go viral, but Joshi says the Interflora team doesn’t operate from a place of chasing likes and comments. “You never design a wedding with the intention of making it go viral; instead, you design knowing it will withstand the emotional weight of the day. It’s never about turning every corner into a photo-op but finding those two or three special spots that naturally become everyone’s favourite backdrop; the places that spark joy and end up living in family albums long after the wedding is over,” she smiles.

article_title: Bridal skincare that works with your hormones, not against them
sub_title: Experts explain how hormones, sleep and nutrition shape your skincare results more than last-minute facials ever could
article_content: The weeks leading up to the wedding can feel like an emotional seesaw: excitement giving way to anxiety, joy interrupted by late-night planning spirals and a constant chorus of advice on what to do (and absolutely not do) as a part of your bridal skincare routine. Slather this, massage that—your skincare arsenal does its thing, but real radiance depends on your gut and hormones running in sync. If skin could ask for one thing in the days leading up to the wedding, Dr Sravya Tipirneni, consultant dermatologist, cosmetologist and trichologist at Manipal Hospitals, Bengaluru, says it would be a simple plea: “Slow down. I need water, sleep and zero new products. Treat me gently; I’m not a dress you can tailor last minute.” "Your skin is essentially a hormone-responsive organ,” says Dr Asha Dalal, director of obstetrics and gynaecology at Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, Mumbai. “Hormones influence almost every layer, from oil production and hydration to According to Dr Dalal, the sweet spot for what people call the “bridal glow” is the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, roughly days six to fourteen. “Oestrogen rises steadily during this period,” she says. “It boosts collagen formation, increases The luteal phase—the seven to ten days before your period—is the moodier half. “Skin is more reactive, oilier and more likely to break out,” she warns, which makes last-minute experimentation risky. Dr Dalal’s rule is straightforward: laser treatments, microneedling and chemical peels should be done four to eight weeks before the wedding, ideally aligned with the follicular phase, when healing is quicker. In her words, a menstrual cycle becomes a beauty calendar when you understand how it behaves. The smallest missteps can snowball. “A night of poor sleep can dull the skin, but a few in a row can spike cortisol enough to slow collagen repair,” says Dr Tipirneni. We often underestimate how fatigue shows up on the face. Over-scheduling only compounds it. “Schedule daily tech-free mental downtime (15–30 minutes) and prioritise 7–9 hours of sleep.” Just as important is restraint. “Implement a strict hands-off rule. It’s the easiest way to keep a tiny blemish from becoming a lasting scar.” Food decides whether the glow holds or falters. Functional medicine nutritionist and lifestyle educator Karishmma Chawla puts it bluntly: “Gluten, dairy, processed foods, sugar, packaged foods with hidden gluten or industrial starch, they don’t vibe with your skin story.” They stoke “Hormones adore high-quality protein,” she says. “When your diet balances proteins and fats well, that’s what shapes your hormone language.” Acne flare-ups, in her framework, are simply messages from the body: a nudge to pay attention. Her “bridal glow grocery list” is a pared-back, functional ritual. Pick up one low-GI fruit (apple, pear, guava, berries or orange), one green ( Cold-pressed coconut oil, herbs and pepper form “a magical concoction” that supports thyroid function, keeps harmful bacteria in check and lends skin a plush finish. Fermented foods—kefir, kombucha, pickled vegetables—enter the picture only when the gut is on steadier ground. Caffeine, meanwhile, is the subtle saboteur. “You don’t have to quit coffee; just stop letting it open the show,” she says. Start the day with lukewarm water and lime or aloe, or go straight to your smoothie, and save your lightest brew for later. Everything eventually finds its way back to cortisol. “Anything that doesn’t align with your gut spikes cortisol because your body thinks danger is near,” Chawla explains. High cortisol steals progesterone—the hormone that soothes—slows thyroid function, alters metabolism and invites bloating, acidity and dullness. “Foods that love you back make your body feel safe.” When the gut is calm, the hormones are steady and the mind is rested, the skin mirrors that peace. The makeup, the facials, the dress–they’re the finishing bows. The radiance underneath is self-built. And as Chawla says, “The outer glow is really just a reflection of the inner healing: food, lifestyle and purpose.”

article_title: Your go-to skincare guide for the ultimate pre-wedding glow up

article_content: Every bride dreams of that unmistakable wedding-day glow, the kind that makes you look effortlessly radiant on your big day. Between fittings, family gatherings, and travel, your skin barely gets a moment to recover. But skincare shouldn’t just sit on the surface—it should work Think of your glow as something that’s built over time. Sure, the facials and organic masks will help, but they can only do so much. Quick fixes may give instant results, but they often don’t last. Beneath the surface, your skin is constantly battling oxidative stress—the invisible damage triggered by pollution, stress, and everyday lifestyle factors. That’s where antioxidants step in. They help neutralise free radicals, support the skin’s natural repair processes, and promote a healthier, more even-toned complexion. While there are many Enter So while you plan your outfit, makeup, and jewellery down to the finest detail, don’t forget the foundation beneath it all: your skin health. Because real glow doesn’t fade when the celebrations end—it follows you into the next exciting chapter of your life.

article_title: How to keep your skin sane through a marathon of destination weddings
sub_title: For wedding guests racing through flights, feasts and shifting climates, with expert advice to keep your skin steady through it all
article_content: On a recent trip to Jaipur for a family wedding, my skin was crying for mercy. Decadent Rajasthani feasts, makeup going on and coming off every few hours, three nights of four-hour sleep and a sudden climate switch turned my face into a cautionary tale. That’s when it struck me that the pursuit of the wedding glow isn’t just the bride’s anymore. Because the modern wedding calendar looks more like a travel itinerary. From Jaisalmer to Jaipur and Phuket to Portofino, your skin is expected to keep up as you hop from one flight to another for more than one happy couple this season. The beauty brief now includes the jet-setting guest, sprinting through ceremonies, red-eye flights and humidity swings, fuelled by equal parts SPF and sheer willpower. As India’s destination weddings evolve into multi-day marathons across climates and time zones, your skincare routine needs to be as versatile and resilient as Athletes train their bodies to run long distances, lift weights to sustain muscle recovery, hydrate well before the big day and get ample rest. Multi-day wedding functions require resilience too. Jet lag shows up on my face. By the time you get off a flight, whatever radiance you have built during the pre-wedding routine has evaporated somewhere over the Arabian Sea. Cabin air steals moisture, circulation slows and that lit-from-within glow fades fast. Add hard hotel water to the mix and the The antidote is a post-flight reset built on deep hydration, soft cleansing and barrier-loving formulas that coax the complexion back to life just in time for the celebrations. Dr Agarwal's go-to ritual: hydrate well, avoid alcohol in flight, cleanse with a rich Different climates rewrite the skin’s entire rulebook. If desert-like heat thins skin barrier, then a shift to a humid weather like Udaipur or Mumbai unfolds the opposite chaos–sweat, sebum and microbes creating a lush playground for congestion and fungal flare-ups. Going up North to places like Delhi and Chandigarh pollution rises, PM levels spike and the skin’s defences work overtime, leaving it inflamed, sensitised and prone to I put a long-standing packing dilemma to the skin experts: if we had room for just five skincare essentials during a destination wedding week, what should make the cut? Here’s what they recommended. Weddings rarely allow for a full routine, but dermatologists agree on the one thing you can’t skip: sunscreen. “Dehydration and breakouts can be fixed, sun damage can’t,” says Dr Agarwal. Another common oversight is failing to adapt products to the climate, and cleansing properly becomes essential. “Makeup wipes aren’t enough. You need water and a real cleanser.” Dr Sethi adds that a stealth culprit behind wedding-fatigue breakouts is the communal brush kit passed around in glam rooms. As indulgent as having on-call makeup artists feel, shared tools are a fast track to acne. My workaround is simple enough. I hand the artist my own brushes, the creativity stays and the breakouts don’t. Ultimately, wedding-season beauty is a test of stamina. The glow chase is no longer the bride's alone, so I’m already getting ready for my next round of destination weddings. If this is an endurance sport, I plan to finish strong.

article_title: When it comes to wedding jewellery, why should women have all the fun?
sub_title: It’s the groom’s time to shine, literally
article_content: When it comes to wedding jewellery, brides have seemingly endless options. So to say, wedding jewellery for men should no longer be an afterthought. “Grooms today are becoming far more experimental and expressive with their jewellery. They are moving beyond the traditional strings of pearls and embracing statement pieces that reflect their personality, be it with a handcrafted kalgi, gemstone buttons or heirloom brooches,” says Sunita Shekhawat, founder and CEO of Sunita Shekhawat. Below, India’s leading jewellery designers get into some classic, other new-age and a few modular jewels for the modern-day groom. Chokers are no longer just the bride’s territory. Grooms are now styling chokers with long necklaces and even ranihaars that elevate their look by many folds. Extra points for colourblocking. Think kanthas, whether monotone or multicoloured, in tumbles of emerald, rubies and other precious gemstones that can be paired with polki chokers. Jadau kamarbandhs are having a moment. Although a tad out there, when it comes to wedding jewellery for men, grooms are styling them on sherwanis to tie up the look. It is a multifunctional piece that can later be used as a necklace by both the bride and the groom. Brooches today come in a wide range of themes, from animal motifs and floral-inspired designs to sleek geometric forms. Polki and jadau brooches featuring striking centre gemstones such as classic rubies and emeralds, as well as playful, vivid stones like lapis and tourmaline, sit really well on neutral-toned sherwanis. They also transition seamlessly into modern wardrobes, making them heirlooms worth investing in. Think beyond the watch. Layer bracelets or kada sets that blend gold with gemstones. It adds a regal touch without feeling overdone. A signet ring is timeless; it carries a strong sense of identity and legacy when customised, engraved with initials, a family crest or studded with a gemstone that resonates with the wearer. It’s a piece that truly becomes a part of you and easily transcends into your occasionwear wardrobe. Choose one statement piece and build around it. For instance, if you’re wearing a heavy necklace, go lighter on the brooch and buttons. Also, make sure your jewellery complements your outfit’s tone–gold for warmer hues and silver or platinum for cooler shades. A sarpech or kalgi is an ornament for the groom’s safa that will always be iconic. It carries an old-world charm and can be passed down for generations to come. One set with uncut diamonds and emeralds can also be pinned on the stole, or later, styled as a brooch.​ A strand of pearls has remained a mainstay in many a bijoux box and for good reason. It is regal, gender-neutral and elegant. Even a string of uncut diamonds works wonders on both neutral and jewel-toned outfits. When they say the devil is in the details, they’re talking about gemstone buttons. Vintage-inspired sherwani buttons encrusted with gemstones of choice make for a regal addition to the groom’s look. While emerald buttons usually take the centre stage, ones with meenakari (coloured enamelling) are also being favoured now. Trust polki cufflinks featuring uncut diamonds or enamel detailing to add a subtle yet regal touch to the groom’s ensemble. Get them engraved with the groom’s initials to make for a bespoke accessory. Pieces that can be detached, adjusted and layered to fit multiple occasions offer versatility that’s second to none. A polki necklace that can be worn as a single statement strand or in layers is a gift that keeps giving. Similarly, sherwani buttons that can be transformed into cufflinks for a more pared-down look for the post-wedding events are ingenious ways to make the most of your jewels. Complement the bride’s jewels and apparel tones without replicating them. And what of the groom’s own fit? Lighter pastels pair beautifully with emeralds and Polki, while deeper hues shine with uncut diamonds or sapphires.

article_title: Your bridal skincare guide for glowing, healthy skin before the wedding
sub_title: If you’re planning your wedding, start planning your skincare too. Here’s Dr Harshna Bijlani’s expert bridal skincare guide, month by month
article_content: You’ve probably curated moodboards, picked your palette and maybe even finalised your dream lehenga and chandbalis. But while the playlists and outfits fall into place, there’s one element that deserves equal attention: your skin. “Your bridal glow is not built in a day,” says Dr Harshna Bijlani, aesthetic physician, celebrity skin expert and founder of AgeLess Clinic. “It’s layered inside out with science, consistency and a little bit of soul care.” With six months to go, the focus is not just on looking flawless but on building a foundation that lasts, starting with lifestyle changes, skincare habits and treatments that work over time. A thoughtful bridal skincare routine begins here. This is the ideal moment to get serious about your skin prep. “The first step is always to fix your foundation, and I don’t mean makeup. I mean your lifestyle,” says Bijlani. She recommends consistent sleep (ideally by 11 pm), cutting back on sugar and dairy if you’re acne-prone, and using sunscreen daily. “Sunscreen is your skincare insurance policy. It protects your treatments, prevents pigmentation and keeps your glow intact.” Begin a personalised routine with actives like vitamin C for brightness, niacinamide to strengthen your barrier and retinoids (if suitable) for smoother texture. You can also start in-clinic treatments such as pigmentation correction through peels, Q-switch lasers or mesotherapy, and The three-month mark is peak treatment season. This window allows enough time for procedures that deliver long-term results but may need recovery. Energy-based options like Ultherapy, Fotona 4D or RF microneedling gradually lift and tone skin, with results appearing closer to the wedding. Regular IV drips containing glutathione, If you’re open to injectables, this is the right time for baby Botox to soften expression lines, subtle fillers for contour and hydration, and skin boosters for luminosity. “The three-month mark is when your skincare routine, workouts and diet need to go on autopilot,” says Bijlani. “Consistency now equals confidence later.” With a month left, avoid new products or aggressive treatments. “Your focus now is on maintenance, hydration and keeping inflammation down,” warns Bijlani. Skip first-time peels, strong actives or lasers. Stick to trusted facials such as hydra facials, LED light therapy and This final stretch is about calming the chaos. Stress and poor sleep can raise cortisol levels, leading to puffiness, dullness and breakouts. Bijlani recommends a simple routine: a gentle double cleanse, a hydrating serum with hyaluronic acid, peptides or ceramides, followed by SPF in the morning and a nourishing barrier cream at night. Cold water dunking can help tone and depuff, while The day before your wedding, give your skin a break. Avoid exfoliants, masks or new products. A gentle hydration mist, barrier cream and nourishing lip balm are enough. Stay away from waxing, shaving or picking at pimples. Use a cold compress if needed and focus on rest. A cup of On your wedding day, simplicity works best. Hydrate, then use only what your skin knows and loves–a mild cleanser, hydrating serum, moisturiser and SPF. Bijlani stresses the importance of at least one makeup trial, ideally a month before. “It’s not just about finalising your look. It’s about testing how your skin reacts to the products, especially base makeup and eyelash glue.” If you plan distinct looks for different events, schedule two separate trials. “More than two can confuse you more than help,” she adds. The calmest brides are always the most radiant. Don’t chase perfection. Focus on balance, breath and feeling beautiful in your own skin. Skincare doesn’t stop at your jawline. What’s on your plate matters as much as what’s in your products. Aim for 2.5 to 3 litres of water daily to keep skin plump and hydrated. Add antioxidant-rich vegetables like carrots, tomatoes and greens, and include Regular movement, breath work and proper sleep complete the picture. Trust the lasers and facials, but also trust the journalling, the tea, the deep breaths before bed. At the heart of every bridal skincare plan is calmness, the kind that no product can replicate.

article_content: For some women, makeup is second nature, the winged liner drawn with the ease of signing one’s name, a lipstick always rolling at the bottom of the handbag, a multi-step skincare-meets-makeup ritual that’s as natural as Then comes the wedding day, when every eye and every camera is on you. Makeup may be part of the day, but it should never make you feel like a stranger in your own Shradha Luthra, a bridal makeup artist, says it all begins with a conversation. “The most important thing to communicate is your comfort level. Tell your artist how much or how little makeup you usually wear. Even if that answer is ‘none’, it gives your artist a baseline. Share what makes you feel most like yourself, whether it is keeping your lips natural or avoiding anything heavy on the eyes. That is the starting point.” Eshwar Log, leading makeup artist, agrees. “Choosing the right makeup artist is everything. Look for someone skilled at skin work and minimal beauty. Have a meeting ahead of time to share your expectations for the wedding day and other events. Even sharing images of looks you do not want helps us understand your taste.” Both experts say skincare is the foundation. “A well-layered routine is key to achieving that glow from within,” says Log. Think lightweight ceramide moisturisers, brightening serums with Log suggests starting early. “Hydrate well, moisturise daily and use SPF. Simple steps that make any makeup sit beautifully on your skin.” The consultation or trial can help the non-makeup bride gain confidence. “It is about understanding each other’s energy,” says Log. “A trial of two looks—a skin-focused one and a subtle glam—helps the bride see how the makeup evolves over a few hours and how it holds up.” The most requested look for brides who rarely wear makeup is the elusive no-makeup makeup. Barely-there tint, soft blush, brushed-up brows and a coat of mascara. Luthra defines it as bridal makeup that feels invisible but is carefully crafted. “Evened-out skin tone, a natural flush, eyes defined just enough to look awake, and lips close to your natural shade—polished but never obvious.” Log adds, “Focus on enhancing one feature: skin, eyes or lips. If it is lips, pick shades that match your undertone, like peach or brown nudes, or a stain topped with gloss. Minimalism does not mean skipping steps. It means thoughtful choices that let the bride shine.” For brides who have never worn makeup, the process can feel daunting. “Explain each step, keep a mirror handy and let the bride see what each product does,” says Log. Music, at a comfortable volume, turns getting ready into a ritual. Luthra adds, “I start with the lightest touches—a hint of blush, sheer “Think of makeup not as a mask but as an enhancer,” says Luthra. article_title: The bridal photography tips every bride needs on her wedding day
sub_title: From what to do with your hands to how to skip stiff poses, here is House on the Clouds founder, Siddharth Sharma's advice that will help you look and feel like yourself
article_content: The wedding décor will be dismantled and the So what do you do when the camera is everywhere, when you are battling humidity, high emotions and twelve-kilo embroidery, and are still expected to look flawless? We built a survival kit of bridal photography tips to help you navigate the day without awkwardness, or worse, your ‘resting stress face’ preserved forever in a high-resolution Google Drive. To do it, we teamed up with Siddharth Sharma, wedding photographer and founder of House on the Clouds, known for his dreamy, cinematic style. He has built a career coaxing nervous brides into looking effortlessly chic. For Sharma, it is not about the perfect angle or smile. His first rule is simple: stop performing. Sharma believes mimicry often dulls authenticity. “There’s no wrong way to be photographed, it’s your day, your personality, and that’s what truly matters,” he says. “The only time things feel off is when brides copy poses that they’ve seen online. That’s when photos can end up looking stiff or unlike you.” He adds that trusting your photographer helps create portraits that feel effortless and timeless: “The best thing is to let your own personality shine through while also trusting your photographer, they’re constantly observing you, your body language and your energy, and they know what will flatter you best.” Nerves show in the hands first. “Hands are sometimes a tricky part of posing but the secret is to give them something natural to do,” says Sharma. He suggests simple movements that feel like you: adjust your When you are juggling heels, emotions and missed calls, the lens can feel invasive. Sharma’s advice is to shift the focus back to the moment: “It is completely normal to feel camera-shy. A lot of brides aren’t used to being photographed this much. But the best way to look natural is to forget the camera sometimes and focus on the moment. Think of it less as posing and more as just being in the moment: small, genuine gestures photograph beautifully.” This mindset underpins his bridal photography tips throughout. Multiple outfit changes might sound exciting in theory, but they can quickly start to feel like a quick-change marathon. Between outfit changes, hair touch-ups and a rapidly ticking schedule, brides often feel like they’re caught in a wardrobe change montage. “The best way to Editing your schedule means you actually get to live in your outfits, not just change in and out of them. It’s better to slow down, savour each look, and give yourself space to enjoy the day. Should you go full Colgate or opt for a subtle Mona Lisa smirk? “The best kind of smile in photos is the one that feels natural to them. There isn’t a rule about showing teeth versus keeping it subtle. It’s more about what looks and feels authentic.”There’s no algorithm for this. You smile like you. That’s where the good photos live. The myth says the ideal bride knows every angle. Sharma disagrees. “The ideal bride is someone who trusts the team she’s hired. Once you’ve chosen your photographer, giving them creative freedom is the best gift you can offer. It makes the entire process flow effortlessly.” As he puts it, “It’s not that much about knowing how to pose or where to look, and more about being present, relaxed and open.” Bridal shoots are not fashion campaigns. Real emotion needs gentle direction. “Posing for models is very different from posing for What separates stiff from timeless often comes down to forgetting the camera. “The best moments happen when couples forget the camera and just enjoy each other,” Sharma says. “When you are present in the moment, the love and ease show up naturally.” Share a private joke, breathe, notice the flowers. The camera will find what is real. So, if anyone offers you cheese in the form of ‘say cheese,’ skip it. Stay real and let the camera catch you. With these bridal photography tips, your wedding album will read like a memory rather than a rehearsal.

article_title: This couple’s botanical wedding was a love letter to ritual, context, and modern grace
sub_title: Shradha and Nagarajan Chandrasekharan’s Bengaluru wedding was a gilded world of meaningful rituals, personal touches and botanical dreams, orchestrated by The Mogra Collective
article_content: Set against the backdrop of the scenic Nandi Hills, Shradha and Nagarajan Chandrasekharan tied the knot in their own special way. Theirs was more than just a union of two people. It was a celebration of their heritage, imbued with modern values. Complementing the heart of each ritual was a riot of colourful blooms and quaint personal touches that invited guests into their world. To put together their dream wedding, this Chennai and Bengaluru-based couple enlisted The Mogra Collective—a boutique event planning firm—renowned for their layered, luxury-focused and design-forward approach. The idea was simple yet profound: to honour their cultural roots while maintaining contemporary sensibilities. What followed was a series of five meticulously-planned events that felt truly personal and moreover, deeply theirs. The For their nuptials, they chose a neutral ritual that paid homage to both their backgrounds, without being shadowed by rigid patriarchal customs. Honouring the bride’s love for all things floral, the team at The Mogra Collective put together an extensive network of flowers around the The celebrations came to a close with a grand, twilight dinner held at Amita Rasa. A pale-green-and-earth-toned affair, the event sparkled with a 100-foot mirrored floor that reflected the hills and the stars. Inspired by Shradha’s sculptural Gaurav Gupta ensemble, this event was designed to exude luxury—a trademark of The Mogra Collective. Soft greens and muted earth tones of the floral palette were chosen to echo both the ensemble and the surrounding landscape. A memorable part of the decor, the 100-foot mirror served as a runway of light and movement. As the day melted into dusk, candlelight, stars, and a spectacular firework display shimmered across its surface. Every detail, from botanical urns to sculpted topiary forms, was calibrated to create a space that felt like a living installation. The five-course menu, curated by Chef Manu Chandra, was a true cherry on top. Spotlighting the couple’s travels and favourite flavours, it created an immersive experience for every guest—bringing them closer to Shradha and Nagarajan Chandrasekharan’s beautiful journey. Shradha, a children’s mental health professional with a passion for policy reform, lent her creative touch by designing her own outfits and rethinking all the stationery. Nagarajan Chandrasekharan, who leads a LiDAR-based technology firm, managed logistics with precision, turning spreadsheets into a quiet kind of art. Working as a team, they drew from each other’s strengths to ensure that their vision was brought to life. From hand-embroidered napkins depicting the couple’s pets to customised menus inspired by their favourite date spots, each element was chosen not to chase trends, but to hold meaning. The outfits, too, were a fitting mix of shimmering Kanjeevarams and elegant Sabyasachis, each with its own personal touch. As Karuna Reddy, founder of The Mogra Collective says, “We don’t design for spectacle. We design for feeling. For context. For story.” This philosophy is precisely why couples turn to them—to bring their stories and visions to life with honesty and authenticity. Every event is approached with precision and a keen eye for detail, making your big day a true reflection of your story—one where love always takes centre stage.

article_title: 16 best wedding destinations for brides who want their venue to match their personality
sub_title: Whether it’s a pristine sandbar in the middle of the Indian Ocean or a family-owned vineyard in the south of France—no matter how unconventional your tastes, we’ve found you a wedding destination to match
article_content: Can there be more to the best wedding destinations than just pretty backdrops to frame one of life’s biggest At this quaint sixth-century château hotel, you’ve got the glamour of the French Riviera but in a bucolic, secluded setting. Indulge in the French art de vivre with excursions to the Riviera, local markets and Provençal villages where you can tailor your celebrations with bespoke wine tastings and the best of gastronomy that the region has to offer. Sign up for a treatment at the award-winning Spa Saint-Martin by La Prairie, that can also be arranged in the hotel’s gardens under a flower-strewn cabana. This stately hotel overlooking the Arno river exudes an old-world charm, thanks in part to the fact that it is a Renaissance-era palace. Weddings here aren’t just opulent, they are also highly personalised—be it an afternoon tea ritual with your closest, a walking tour in the city guided by an art historian or events at venues with grand frescoes and gilded ceilings within the property. Ask the concierge team to put together a romantic dinner on the historic Ponte Vecchio bridge or set up a picnic at sunset for your family. Nestled inside 20 acres of gardens lined with olive and fruit trees, this palace hotel has hosted everyone from Alfred Hitchcock to Moroccan royalty in its century-long existence. There are grand salons in which to host parties and traditional Moroccan or Nhaza-style picnics and hammams to relax in with your bridesmaids. If you do somehow end up with time to spare, ask the concierge team to curate a visit to the local souks and medina, or an insider’s tour of the city on vintage motorcycles. This hotel might be contemporary in design but it is steeped in the cultural nuances of Kyoto. The an 800-year-old heritage pond garden at its heart forms the pièce de résistance for a tranquil wedding celebration. Culinary experiences are a big focus: the chefs can design custom menus for a relaxed welcome dinner or a farewell brunch. Thrill your guests with thoughtful, hands-on experiences—whether it’s a workshop in kintsugi (the Japanese art of mending ceramics with gold) or a quiet tea ceremony led by a local tea master. Framed by pine-clad mountain slopes, green meadows and snow-capped peaks, this 85-key boutique ski resort makes for an intimate escape with your closest—especially if food drives much of your relationship. Let the landscaped gardens and breathtaking views from the amphitheatre lawns act as the backdrop for your picture-perfect wedding, while you savour an authentic wazwan spread­—and then head to The Khyber Spa by L’Occitane to recover. For those interested in a tasteful wedding without too much flash and bang, this heritage family-run property offers the perfect mix of quiet charm and refined elegance, paired with bespoke dining destinations and renowned local boutiques and jewellery stores. Trust the team to tailor a wedding celebration after your heart, whether it’s a sit-down dinner for 100 guests featuring classic Rajasthani delicacies or a large meet-and-greet at the majestic Amarbagh ballroom. Everything about this 16th-century palace hotel, just 45 kms from Jaipur, speaks restrained glamour. It remains one of the finest examples of Indo-Saracenic architecture; its vintage charm preserved in hand-painted murals, bougainvillea-fringed courtyards and terrace gazebos. Sheesh Mahal is the crown jewel, featuring hundreds of hand-cut mirrors, jewel-toned glass work and delicate frescoes—an apt setting for that one big reception you want after a quick court wedding, ending in a spectacular display of fireworks. Is your wedding just an excuse to unwind in the midst of nature with your inner circle? Consider this boutique resort overlooking the backwaters of the Moira River. Here you’ll find a curated selection of rooms and villas with plunge pools—the perfect canvas for an intimate wedding where you’re surrounded by a forest and the sound of birdsong. The villa and poolside lawns make for a breezy setting for your nuptials and reception, while the Storii Lounge can host a a quiet welcome dinner or mehendi celebration. For adventure lovers, this boutique safari camp in Rajasthan’s leopard country offers unbridled luxury. With just 10 tented suites, the entire property can be your canvas for an intimate, unusual celebration—where guests can be treated to breakfast in the wild, sundowners by the lake, wildlife safaris, a walk with a Rabari herdsman and dinners in the company of folk musicians under starlit skies surrounded by the soft glow of thousands of lanterns. Imagine hosting your wedding at one of the largest natural islands in the UAE, where you get a vantage view of free-roaming wildlife. At this luxury resort, with just 30 pool villas overlooking the savannah (and gazelles grazing in the distance), host a cozy cocktail soiree in the wadi, enjoy a barbecue under the stars, say your vows at the beach at sunset and throw in a few safari experiences—life moves at its own pace here, promising a wedding unlike anywhere else. Set on the fringes of the Siswan forest, this sprawling resort with a striking traditional façade, serene gardens, fountains and reflection pools offers luxurious tented accommodation as well as rooms. Have your guests make the most of the tranquil beauty with guided treks and forest trails, raise a toast under the stars on the private poolside deck with glasses of bubbly and canapés and indulge in farm-to-fork dining and authentic Punjabi fare. Looking to truly go off-the-grid for your wedding? How about this far-flung private island resort in the middle of the Indian Ocean which involves chartering a 25-minute flight? At this resort in East Africa, there are just 50 private pool villas and abundant barefoot luxury. Ask the concierge team to plan things for you—whether it’s sunset pheras overlooking the ocean, chartering a catamaran or paddle boarding with sea turtles. It could be the adventure of a lifetime. This 200-year-old fort turned boutique hotel boasts an impressive Jaipur gharana-style architecture—a great backdrop for your wedding. What’s more: the resort’s practices are rooted in sustainability, from the use of natural elements like local flowers, upcycled materials and earthen lamps in wedding decor, to encouraging guests to plant trees. Give your wedding party a sensorial experience with rooftop dinners, riverbed walks, village safaris and sunset high teas. This newly opened hotel, with its water conservation practices and use of live food counters instead of buffets to lower food wastage, is a perfect example of how luxury and sustainability can coexist. The spectacular Chand Baori, inspired by Rajasthan’s stepwells, would be great for your pheras; and there are several terraces to host a mehfil by moonlight. Spring for the Fairmont thaal experience—a feast showcasing lost Rajasthani recipes and heirloom cooking techniques. Designed as an homage to the sacred water palaces of Java, Jumeirah Bali is an elegant all-villa beach resort that captures the allure of island living. They prioritise seasonal menus, sustainably sourced produce, low-waste and plastic-free decor, compostable florals and supporting local artisans with guest-driven experiences like making Balinese ceremonial offerings and personalised Batik art. Couple that with luxurious accommodation and sweeping views of the ocean for a truly immersive experience. Weddings at this 19th-century manor—overlooking vine-covered terraces and the Douro river—are enhanced by their sustainable practices, such as the use of seasonal produce in their curated menus and upcycled materials in decor. Plan your nuptials under the shade of ancient olive trees in the garden, have your guests indulge in private wine tastings with local vintners or attend workshops in making their own cosmetics with local ingredients and essential oils—these memories will be etched in time.

article_title: 26 engagement nails to try with celebrity inspiration
sub_title: From timeless neutrals to bold designs, these engagement nail ideas will have your ring finger ready for its close-up
article_content: Engagement nails are often minimalist–think French manicures or neutral shades–which makes sense in the era of Instagram announcement posts, with your ring finger hand on full display, says celebrity manicurist Tom Bachik, whose clientele includes Jennifer Lopez and Selena Gomez. But it's your special day (or, the run-up to your special day), so we say the rules are yours to make. Nail artist Brittney Boyce counts Olivia Rodrigo, Megan Fox and Kim Kardashian as regular clients, and she reports seeing more experimentation with colour and design. The best engagement nail, she says, is the one you love. “This all just comes down to personal style,” she says. For some, that's a short natural nail. For others, it's the Swarovski-encrusted nails JLo recently wore (scroll on for the inspiration, of course). So whether you’ve already found your forever person or are still using those crystals to attract him, her, or them into your life, it’s never too early to start brainstorming. Below are 27 engagement nail ideas to get those glam creative juices flowing. You’ll need this for when you book that nail salon appointment. A throwback to Margot Robbie's Oscar nails in 2021, manicurist Tom Bachik went with a natural shade. If you want length but don't have natural nails, try Apres Gel-X Extensions. When it comes to engagement manicures, neutral shades are foolproof—they match everything. This creamy tan acrylic will make any engagement ring stand out. But as with any mani, good grooming is essential. If you’re seeking a subtle design to elevate a bare base, opt for the classic French mani. Bachik painted thick white lines along the tips of Nicola Peltz Beckham’s long square nails for a dynamic look. We’re all about metallic sheens, but there’s something really warm about bronze. Choose this if you’re looking to put a unique spin on a basic bare or brown nail shade. Looking for some colour? Vibrant and alluring, Bachik’s cherry red nail look on Michelle Williams makes for the ideal engagement mani. Another subtle way to dress up any mani is with tiny nail art details, as seen here on JLo. We love Bachik’s addition of a small silver curve hugging the bottom of the French tip for an unexpected spin on a timeless look. More Jennifer Lopez inspo. This rich chocolate brown with grey undertones not only makes for a great neutral nail, but it also provides the perfect contrast to coloured engagement rings. Her green diamond just pops. It may seem too on-the-nose to wear white engagement nails before you get proposed to. But there’s no arguing that white nails make your engagement ring shine a tiny bit more. (Plus, there’s nothing wrong with expecting that ring; gotta manifest!). For just a hint of chrome, dress your French mani with textured silver tips. As a base, Boyce likes to use a milky neutral over something opaque and recommends something like the Aprés Nail’s Colour Extend Gel Bottle in Carla. Married lady Jennifer Lopez wore these Swarovski nails in her This modern take on a nail trend popular in the 1940s feels crisp and fresh—a bit of nail art, but nothing to distract from the main attraction. For something more unexpected and trendy, mix white and black streaks for a bolder engagement nail. Set these designs against a bare nail to ground the look. This super-shiny mani has a bit of edge in just the way we like it. Ethereal and romantic, milk bath nails evoke inviting calm and a sense of wanderlust (and they’re super-pretty). Blake Lively wears a creamy milk bath base with delicately placed floral decals that accentuate her ring. This Tiffany blue is a rich turquoise with a glossy sheen that will take your IG engagement photo to the next level. In true “quiet luxury” fashion, Sofia Richie Granger wears her natural short nails with her engagement ring. If you want to keep it bare but still polished, swipe on a clear coat like the OPI Brilliant High-Shine Top Coat, or the Dior Nail Glow Polish that gives you a hint of pink. Once upon a time, the black mani was reserved for Halloween and/or angsty teens. No longer: black nails are a modern classic, and one of the chicest options for an engagement nail look. Just take a cue from Kourtney Kardashian. Dark, edgy, yet still very much romantic—we’re here for it. If you’re still looking to get that glazed doughnut-inspired look, add some iridescent shine. Serena Williams goes for sparkly light pink nails that shine bright like her engagement ring. Ciara proves that mauve makes for a great go-to nail colour. The mix of purple and pink with cool undertones works for every skin tone. We love this warm gold-orange shade Beyoncé sports. It’s got sheer coverage and a light metallic sheen that doesn’t overpower the stunning ring on her finger. The creamy shade of this Essie pink polish (it's Bubble Away, a classic shade) is bold but still feels like a neutral. This is basically the red nail theory’s final boss (if you subscribe to that philosophy, of course). Celebrity nail artist Julie Kandalec credits one of her clients for the idea and describes it as “a deep brick-ish red with white chrome over it.” Striking yet chic, there’s nothing like a classic red to pair with your new ring. A look Kandalec recently did for Emily Blunt, this cool-toned champagne nail with silver French tips is an easy way to elevate a classic mani. (And we're loving the ever-popular almond-shaped nail that just elongates the fingers). Mixing two different shades in the same colour family can add some needed dimension and depth to your engagement nails. “Subtle, yet visually very interesting close up,” says Kandalec of the look. A two-toned nail is a classic (and easy to do, which is always a major plus). With its velvety feel and mesmerising shimmers, cat-eye nails are one of the most fun looks you can try—especially for an engagement mani. Either go all out with a full cat-eye or find a happy medium. Kandalec recommends a more subtle variation and suggests starting up top with the cat-eye effect before gradually transitioning it to a more neutral shade at the base. Looking for a deep infusion of colour? Kandalec says to go for jewel tones. “They’re rich in tone and luxurious,” she says. Her favourite is a cranberry red. But you can also opt for a deep emerald or purple to really make your engagement nails pop.

article_title: 26 marriage tips to keep the spark alive long after ‘I do’
sub_title: The best weddings might be straight out of fairy tales, but the best marriages are fuelled by hard work, deep wells of patience and abundant empathy
article_content: The most enchanting weddings often feel like they’ve leapt straight out of a fairy tale, with glittering lights, tear-jerking vows and storybook romance. But once the confetti has run out and the cake has been eaten, the marriage that truly begins—a commitment that’s built on something far deeper. The strongest marriages demand hard work, the kind that shows up even when it’s inconvenient. Because while weddings may sparkle, it’s the quiet, consistent tending of love that makes a marriage last. Below, So you’re a double income household run by a power couple with soaring careers and sky-high ambitions? Between income-based power play, stealth overspending and a mismatch in financial values, “The sage Vatsayana wrote that for good sex, the genitals have to be fairly matching in size,” says mythologist and author of Begin by “sharing what family means to you from a space of understanding context, not from a space of blame,” suggests Mumbai-based psychotherapist Anusha Manjani. “In South Asia, we marry into networks of duty and history. Often what we call ‘interference’ by in-laws is unresolved enmeshment or unconscious loyalty. Partners are often trying to mature from fused roles like the ‘good child’, ‘dutiful son’, ‘obedient daughter-in-law’ and that can create conflict.” So what can you do about this? “Keep the focus on ‘we’—align as a team and be clear on what is okay and not okay when it comes to spending time with family. For example, how do we want to spend our holidays and festivals?” Come to this conversation not with rigid expectations, but patience while being firm and clear. “Think of this not as rebellion, but repair.” To begin with, says Mohan, pre-nups are not legally recognised in India and can get thrown out of court easily. And secondly, wouldn’t you rather enter a marriage, even one with a wealth imbalance, with openness and clarity? “This may be unsettling, but you’d rather do the hard work of tackling wealth planning early on,” says Mohan. “And if your partner or partner’s family is the one insisting on legalities, don’t be dismissive or look at it as an accusation. Try to understand what’s going on instead and consult your own lawyers on the whys and the whats. This is where you really get to know who you’re marrying, so don’t take this experience for granted.” Between endless tasks, a mountain of paperwork and a million Zoom calls (that could’ve been an email), it can be hard to take out time for each other when you’re both at work. Harder still when there’s an Instagram reel or Twitter storm always at hand to distract you. “Little updates during breaks like ‘I just ate’ or ‘having such a tough day’ can help you stay connected even when you’re apart,” says New Delhi-based psychologist Divija Bhasin. Memes or emoji work too, if those are your love language. Screens in bed and when we wake up—who are we really married to? “Create intentional screen free rituals,” says Manjani. “Ask them: what was especially joyful or challenging about your day?” It could be at a device-free dinner, while making a cup of coffee or reconnecting at the end of the day while doing chores. “It is not about the amount of time or money spent on dates but more about creating room for daily presence and connection with each other.” Anand recommends carving out 15 minutes at the end of every day for “very close, intimate, non sex time” and building it into your daily routine. “Lie down with each other naked and cuddle but don’t talk about sexy stuff. Talk about your day. The rule is, this does not lead to sex. This is to remind yourself how good and comforting and nice it feels to touch each other, to truly be with each other.” Of course, it isn’t fair that one partner becomes the default chef/maid/ house manager if the other is on a faster growth trajectory. “Sit down to ask: What does a functioning home look like to both of us? What tasks do we hate? What do we not mind? What can we afford to outsource so we don’t end up totally hating each other?” says Mohan. You can also draw up a joint chore schedule. “One person has late-night meetings on Tuesdays? Cool—maybe the other handles dinner that day and they swap on Friday. The idea is to be equitable (different from equal).” Maybe you’re so swamped with your partner track, you actually can’t do the laundry. “But then, perhaps you can handle all the bill payments or weekend grocery runs,” says Mohan. “The point is to demonstrate intent and to say, ‘I see this as our shared load and I want to carry my part’.” Anand suggests practising “relationship foreplay”. The key to good intimacy, she says, is transition: You have to be in the right frame of mind, not still thinking about that email you’re drafting or that contract you need to sign. She suggests watching a comedian together in bed (and naked, if you like) because “you can’t imagine what laughing together can do for your relationship.” Or the very tactile, sensory act of cooking. “Either you turn it into a game or it’s just a simple meal,” says Anand. “Think about the transitions that you actually use so it’s not like cooking with a friend.” “We all have core needs of being seen and heard, and listening with intention and attention is a big part of what is needed to build intimacy today,” says Manjani. A screen-less weekend can do wonders, she says: Stay in and read to each other or play strip Scrabble, go out and explore the city, but take time away from work and your screens. It can “ground, reconnect and bring more care to what the relationship needs”. Hit the padel court, go hiking once a week, ride the Peloton—whatever it is, make a habit of getting out of the house and into spaces where you can kick things up a notch, even allow your competitive side to come out and play. “Anything other than that mandatory weekly candlelight dinner date which comes with so much pressure to perform,” says Anand. They love going on road trips with their friends, you could spend the whole weekend knitting through re-runs of It’s never easy: An unexpected anxiety attack while getting ready for work or living under a black cloud for weeks. It’s not easy on them—or you. “But try to learn more about your partner’s mental health problems by reading about it,” says Bhasin. “We often tell people to be positive or be grateful to try and cheer them up but can end up invalidating their feelings in the process.” Instead, seek professional help but also understand that actually taking that help will be their call. “A long hug, holding their hand during a tough conversation, placing your palm gently on their back or leaning into each other can signal ‘I’m here with you, I care for you, I see you’ to your partner’s nervous system,” says Manjani. Maybe you don’t want sex after a harrowing week at work, but you do want… something. Set a 15-minute timer for judgement-free play, says Anand, and tell them to give you the neck massage or kisses on your stomach that you’ve been craving. Or, maybe you don’t like how they kiss you. Lack of courage, meet role-play. “A friend in the kink community came up with this wonderful idea,” says Anand, “try light sub and dom play. It’s like a verbal script where you basically issue directions. Plus, you can be sure that your partner is listening at this point because, I’m sorry to say, but a lot of the time they are not.” The reality of contemporary life is that we assess the world (and ourselves) in terms of productivity and can end up assigning value based on numbers. Manjani sees a lot of couples “keeping track of who did what or earned how much”. “It is important to use a shared language of respect and not comparison when talking about time and contribution. Try to name—and value the invisible labour and reclaim rest.” Sex toys, says Anand, are great to experiment with together because “they can help take the pressure off and then this time can just be for the sheer pleasure of being together. On days when you’re not up to it, it’s wonderful to have mutual masturbation.” And if all of that is too uncomfortable, then play with toys by yourself, she says, without the guilt. “The more you understand your body, the more you can guide your partner. It’s not their job to discover your pleasure points.” Maybe it’s real estate, or maybe it’s a joint retirement fund that you will sink into that round-the-world cruise you’ve dreamt of your whole life—but creating a long-term asset or goal together, says Mohan, is a powerful way of showing commitment. “You want to convey that the money you make is not ‘your’ money, but ‘our’ money. If you’re the earning or significantly higher earning partner, proactively include your partner in your financial decision-making process so he or she feels like you’re working towards a joint future.” Things change. You change. You might have realised you aren’t enjoying something you thought you were flexible about—or the opposite. Anand suggests having monthly talks about boundaries which, just like consent, is not a one-time thing set in stone—and this isn’t even restricted to sex. To make it a conversation, not confrontation, Anand and her partner would gather daisies on walks in the meadows behind their house, and then offer a daisy to each other for each new rule they wanted to set. “Create a ritual. It softens the edges.” Every once in a while, leave them a note noticing the everyday or unsaid gestures, says Manjani. Things like “thank you for always making me laugh at awkward family gatherings” or “thank you for making the reservations whenever we go out to eat.” They’ll love that you’re paying attention. Think you might be bisexual? Want to try cuckolding? “Don’t go try it and then come back and say, I enjoyed that,” says Anand. “You have to remember that marriage is like a contract that you sign. There are certain unwritten rules and the main one of monogamy is fidelity.” Talk about it with your partner, she says—you might be surprised at just how willing they are to go along with it. If you or your partner want to try polyamory or an open marriage, Anand’s advice is to look up the subject to understand what questions need to be asked. “It’s not as simple as deciding that one wants to also sleep with somebody else at the same time. There are some basic questions you need to deal with that don’t even fall in the emotional paradigm—things like STIs, living arrangements, financial arrangements, legal repercussions. Remember: this requires even higher levels of trust than being monogamous.” Maybe it’s not even Tinder; maybe they’re just talking—to ChatGPT. “Even though AI can become a proxy for unmet needs, the actual work is in facing what those needs are—was it emotional availability, curiosity, lack of judgement or distraction? Is it a symptom of loneliness or disconnection, or is one partner trying to reclaim something they have lost—desire, aliveness or validation? In therapy, we don’t rush to close or repair the relationship but create space to understand these needs and check if it is possible to reconnect and repair,” says Manjani. “Create time to check in with the other,” says Manjani. “Ask: do you need Comfort (need for support and rest), Connection (time to spend together, affection, touch) or Celebration (need to be appreciated or to celebrate a small win)?” And then follow through with action, however small. On one side is rhythm and habit (or worst case, total monotony). On the other is discovery and reconnection. “Try new things: dance or doodle, introduce your favourite childhood games and activities to each other,” suggests Manjani. “Find ways to create joy—because that joy is glue.

article_title: A Rajkot wedding inspired by travel, heritage, and a touch of retro glam
sub_title: Naiya and Sidd Chhayani’s wedding had strong Gujarati influences alongside picturesque backdrops and 1920s elegance
article_content: Their first date in Boston unfolded without pretence—two creative spirits talking about travel, culture, food, and their shared love for dogs. That conversation marked the beginning of a relationship shaped by curiosity and connection. Over the next two years, Naiya and Sidd explored the world together, turning travel dreams into shared memories and strengthening their bond with every adventure. It was there that they decided their story would return to Rajkot, Gujarat, where love, heritage, and artistry would converge in a wedding captured by Planning a wedding across continents required the couple to make multiple trips to India. From selecting the floral arrangements and curating exquisite menus to working directly with artisans, every decision was guided by their vision. The process, though meticulous, was filled with joy. Their advice to other couples: “Enjoy the process and don’t get lost in the details. Communicate, set realistic expectations, and remember it’s about celebrating your love.” The festivities began at Regency Lagoon Resort, Rajkot. The mehndi ceremony, enhanced with green accents and tropical arrangements, echoed the couple’s love for cultural detail. The following day, the haldi and sangeet unfolded with a Greek-inspired aesthetic—blue and sunlit yellow elements setting a festive tone. Guests embraced the colour palette, while the couple stood out in striking pink tie-dye. By nightfall, the sangeet transformed into a Bollywood-inspired celebration, complete with custom posters, a red-carpet entrance, a Filmfare-style frame, and spirited performances from friends and family. The wedding ceremony itself was envisioned as a balance of tradition and contemporary design. A pastel palette, accented with peach, softened the grandeur, while floral installations, reminiscent of Singapore’s Gardens by the Bay, evoked the couple’s shared passion for travel. The groom, dressed in regal attire with a sharply tailored ivory sherwani paired with a white turban and a ceremonial sword, channelled a maharaja-inspired ensemble. His arrival began in a vintage Rolls-Royce before he mounted a white horse for the final stretch, accompanied by dhol, a live DJ, and dancing. The bride wore a crimson lehenga, embroidered with zari and resham. Her look was completed by traditional jewellery and a Sabyasachi mangalsutra with a lion motif—an auspicious symbol of strength and prosperity in Gujarati culture. While the ceremony was steeped in tradition, the couple introduced intimate Western elements: handwritten vows and the bride walking down the aisle with a white bouquet in hand. The reception shifted into a world of retro glamour. Black-and-gold decor, sweeping gowns, and tuxedos set the tone for a celebration reminiscent of the Great Gatsby era. Champagne toasts and high-energy performances by the newlyweds and their loved ones brought the festivities to a dazzling close—a fitting finale to a wedding that honoured both heritage and modernity.
